docs.title: MTUOC: A Practical Course on Machine Translation Technologies
docs.text:
Welcome to this open online course on practical machine translation technologies that introduces learners to the use of MTUOC, a modular ecosystem of open-source tools designed to make machine translation workflows more accessible to translators, language professionals, teachers, researchers and students. The course is organised into four modules:

  1. Deployment, Integration and Evaluation
  2. Corpus Engineering
  3. NMT Training and Fine-tuning
  4. LLMs for Translation

This course has been developed by:

  • Antoni Oliver Universitat Oberta de Catalunya aoliverg@uoc.edu

  • Sergi Alvarez-Vidal Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona sergi.alvarez@uab.cat

To begin, go to About This Course or How to Navigate This Course.

docs.title: About this Course
docs.text:
MTUOC: A Practical Course on Machine Translation Technologies is an open online course designed to introduce learners to practical machine translation technologies through the MTUOC ecosystem.

Machine translation is now part of many professional translation, localisation and multilingual communication workflows. However, many open-source machine translation and large language model tools require technical knowledge that may be unfamiliar to translators, language professionals and students in the humanities. This course addresses that gap by offering a practical, guided and accessible introduction to machine translation technologies.

The course focuses on MTUOC, a modular ecosystem of open-source tools designed to make machine translation workflows easier to deploy, evaluate, integrate and adapt. Through a set of step-by-step activities, learners will explore how machine translation systems can be used, evaluated and connected to professional translation environments.

The course is organised into four modules:

  1. Deployment, Integration and Evaluation Learners will explore how to start machine translation systems, use MTUOC Server, connect MT systems to translation workflows and evaluate translation output with automatic metrics.

  2. Corpus Engineering This module introduces the preparation, cleaning, alignment and conversion of linguistic data for machine translation purposes.

  3. NMT Training and Fine-tuning Learners will work with neural machine translation workflows, including model training, adaptation and deployment.

  4. LLMs for Translation This module introduces the use of large language models in translation-related workflows, including prompt-based translation and fine-tuning approaches.

The course is aimed at translation students, language professionals, teachers, researchers and anyone interested in understanding how machine translation technologies work in practice. No advanced programming background is required, although learners should be willing to work with digital tools, follow technical instructions and experiment with command-line environments when needed.

By the end of the course, learners will be able to:

  • understand the main components of a machine translation workflow;
  • deploy and test machine translation systems using MTUOC tools;
  • evaluate machine translation output with automatic metrics;
  • prepare and manage linguistic resources for machine translation;
  • understand the basic logic of neural machine translation training and fine-tuning;
  • explore the role of large language models in translation workflows;
  • critically reflect on the possibilities and limitations of machine translation technologies.

docs.title: About the Authors
docs.text:

Holding a PhD in Linguistics and a background in Telecommunications Engineering, his research focuses on Machine Translation, Computational Linguistics, terminology extraction, and natural language processing. He has authored numerous open-source tools for translation and parallel corpus creation, such as LitPC and TBXTools. His research is widely published in high-impact international journals such as Language Resources and Evaluation, Procesamiento del Lenguaje Natural, Tradumàtica, and Linguamàtica, as well as top computational linguistics conferences like EAMT, EACL, and the Machine Translation Summit. Contact: aoliverg@uoc.edu

Sergi Alvarez Vidal is an Assistant Professor at Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (UAB) specializing in Translation Technology, Computational Linguistics, and Machine Translation. His primary research focuses on the empirical evaluation of Machine Translation (MT) and its integration into professional workflows, with a strong emphasis on low-resource languages like Catalan and Aranese. He actively participates in competitive research projects, including TAN-IBE, TamTAS, and Generatese2LT. His work is published in journals such as Mutatis Mutandis, Linguamàtica, Ampersand, Language and Law / Linguagem E Direito, Perspectives and Revista Tradumàtica. docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
To complete the practical activities in this course, you should:

  • have basic computer literacy;
  • be comfortable downloading and installing software;
  • be willing to follow step-by-step technical tutorials.

No previous programming experience is required.

Some practical activities require Docker Desktop and other software components. Installation instructions are provided when they are first needed in the course.

docs.title: Course Structure
docs.text:
The course is organised into four thematic modules. Each module follows a similar structure to help you progress through the course.

A typical module includes:

  • an introduction to the topic;
  • learning objectives;
  • learning materials;
  • practical tutorials;
  • hands-on activities;
  • a self-assessment quiz;
  • additional resources, where appropriate.

The course is self-paced, but we recommend completing the modules in order, as each module builds on concepts introduced previously.

docs.title: Module 1. Deployment, Integration and Evaluation
docs.text:
Welcome to Module 1 of the course. This module covers the deployment of machine translation engines, their integration into professional CAT tools, and the evaluation of NMT models and Large Language Models (LLMs).

  • 1. The MTUOC project

  • Core ecosystem, server architecture, installation, and basic usage.

  • 2. Open Neural Machine Translation models

  • Deployment and usage of open-source NMT architectures such as OpusMT and NLLB.

  • 3. Integration into CAT tools

  • Connecting MTUOC server with professional translation software including OmegaT and Trados.

  • 4. Large Language Models and translation

  • Overview and application of LLMs within machine translation workflows.

  • 5. Large Language models integration into MTUOC server

  • Practical integration of open LLMs (such as SalamandraTA and Gemma) into local pipelines.

  • 6. Summary and Self-Assessment

  • Global review of Module 1 concepts and self-assessment evaluation.

docs.title: 1. The MTUOC Project
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this section, you should be able to:

  • Understand the main components of the MTUOC ecosystem and their role in machine translation workflows.

  • Explain how MTUOC-server connects NMT systems and LLMs with client applications, including CAT tools.

  • Identify the main features of MTUOC-server for integrating translation technologies into professional workflows.

  • Configure, run, test, and manage MTUOC-server using the command line, the graphical interface, and MTUOC recipes.

To gain a deeper foundational knowledge of the MTUOC project and its server architecture, we recommend reading the following academic papers:

  • Antoni Oliver and Sergi Alvarez-Vidal (2023). Training and integration of neural machine translation with MTUOC. In Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Open Community-Driven Machine Translation, pages 5–13, Tampere, Finland. European Association for Machine Translation.

docs.title: 1.1. Overview of the MTUOC Project
docs.text:
The MTUOC project, developed at the Arts and Humanities Department of the Universitat Oberta de Catalunya (UOC), is a comprehensive open-source initiative designed to facilitate the training, customization, use, and integration of neural machine translation (NMT) and statistical machine translation (SMT) systems, as well as Large Language Models (LLMs) for translation, within professional translation environments.

While most modern MT toolkits are distributed under free and open licenses, their practical adoption in real-world professional workflows presents several challenges:

  • Technical Skills Barrier: Toolkits often require medium-to-high programming knowledge (Python, Bash scripting) and may lack comprehensive, user-friendly documentation.
  • Integration and Interoperability: Custom-trained engines cannot always be easily or natively integrated into popular Computer-Assisted Translation (CAT) tools used by professional translators.
  • Hardware Requirements: While training new NMT models requires powerful dedicated GPUs and significant RAM, running inference — translating text with an already trained model — requires considerably fewer computational resources.

MTUOC addresses these issues by providing well-documented scripts, accessible graphical user interfaces, and a highly configurable local server. All project components are distributed under a free GNU GPL license, allowing individual professionals, language service providers (LSPs), and educational organizations to maintain technological independence and data confidentiality.

docs.title: 1.2. Key Ecosystem Components
docs.text:
The project provides a comprehensive ecosystem of modular tools covering different stages of the machine translation lifecycle:

  • Corpus Creation: Utilities designed to extract and convert proprietary translation formats (such as TMX, SDLTM, and XLIFF) into plain tabular text files. The project includes automated programs for sentence-level document alignment using Hunalign, as well as tools for comparable corpus mining using sentence embeddings with SBERT.
  • Corpus Cleaning and Combination: Advanced scripts to remove HTML/XML formatting tags, normalize special characters, filter out corrupt segments by length ratios, and verify language identification using fasttext. An algorithm to clean and rescore large parallel corpora is also available. Additionally, the project includes utilities to expand specialized domain corpora by retrieving similar segments from large general corpora based on language model perplexity.
  • Preprocessing and Training: Standardized data preparation tools, including tokenizers, truecasers, and subword segmentation models such as BPE and SentencePiece. The project provides pre-configured training scripts and configuration files for engines such as Moses, Marian, OpenNMT, and Eole, as well as step-by-step guides and scripts to fine-tune open LLMs specifically for translation tasks.
  • Free Pre-trained Engines: The project packages and distributes pre-trained, ready-to-use NMT models for several language pairs and specialized domains.
  • Client Programs: Dedicated desktop applications and a web interface for translating standalone documents are distributed with the suite. A specialized post-editing environment is also under active development.

docs.title: 1.3. The MTUOC-Server
docs.text: MTUOC-server is a central component of the architecture, designed specifically to address the interoperability gap between backend machine translation engines and frontend professional CAT tools.

docs.title: 1.3.1. Architecture and Workflow
docs.text:
The server operates on a lightweight client-server model, acting as a middleware bridge. The translation workflow follows a clear multi-step process:

  1. Request: The client application (e.g., a CAT tool plugin or translation desktop application) sends a source segment to MTUOC-server.
  2. Preprocessing: The server preprocesses the incoming segment by applying the required pipeline (tokenization, truecasing, subword segmentation with SentencePiece, etc.).
  3. Inference: The server forwards the processed segment to the underlying MT engine or local/remote LLM.
  4. Postprocessing: After receiving the translated output from the engine, the server applies the corresponding inverse processing steps (detokenization, undoing subword splits, character re-normalization, etc.).
  5. Response: The final clean translated segment is formatted and returned to the client.

docs.title: 1.3.2. Protocol Interoperability
docs.text:
One of the key features of MTUOC-server is its ability to communicate using multiple protocols, including MTUOC, Moses, ModernMT, OpenNMT, and NMTWizard. The server can emulate these protocols, and new protocols can be added in the future.

For instance, you can use a fast Marian neural engine while configuring MTUOC-server to behave like a Moses server. This makes it possible to integrate different translation engines with CAT tools and other client applications without requiring them to support each underlying engine directly.

docs.title: 1.3.3. Supported Systems and LLMs
docs.text:
The server supports a broad range of translation technologies:

  • NMT Systems: Open-source engines and models such as Marian, OpenNMT, Moses, OpusMT, NLLB, CTranslate2, and Apertium, as well as commercial APIs such as DeepL and Google Translate.
  • Large Language Models (LLMs): The server integrates models such as Salamandra, Bloom, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Tower. Users can access these models via API or by downloading models from Hugging Face and running them locally using the transformers library. The server also allows users to define custom translation prompts and use regular expressions to extract the translated text from the LLM response.

docs.title: 1.3.4. Features for Professional Workflows
docs.text:
To support professional translation workflows, MTUOC-server includes several advanced features:

  • XML/HTML Tag Restoration: Neural engines may struggle to place formatting tags correctly, for example when processing DOCX files. The server uses an algorithm based on word or subword alignments from the MT system to restore tags. If the MT system does not provide alignments, external fast_align models can be used.
  • Translation Memories: The server can integrate translation memories and return a translation memory match when its similarity score exceeds a predefined threshold.
  • CAT Tool Plugins: Dedicated plugins are available for direct integration with OmegaT and RWS Trados Studio.

docs.title: 1.3.5. Hardware and Platform Compatibility
docs.text: MTUOC-server is multiplatform and runs on Linux, Windows, and macOS. While training MT systems requires powerful hardware, running MTUOC-server for translation does not necessarily require a GPU. It can run on standard consumer computers, making NMT and LLM technology more accessible while allowing translators to keep client data on their local machines.

docs.title: 1.4.1. Getting MTUOC-Server, Versions and Prerequisites
docs.text:
To get MTUOC-server, go to the MTUOC-server GitHub repository.

If you have a Python 3 interpreter installed on your system, you can use the Python source code and install the required dependencies listed in requirements.txt.

Alternatively, you can go to the Releases section and download the binary version for your operating system.

docs.title: 1.4.2. Running MTUOC-Server from the Terminal
docs.text:
To start MTUOC-server using the default config-server.yaml configuration file, enter the following command in the terminal:

python3 MTUOC-server.py

If you want to use a specific configuration file, for example config-server-opusmt-eng-spa.yaml, use:

python3 MTUOC-server.py config-server-opusmt-eng-spa.yaml

To stop MTUOC-server, enter:

python3 MTUOC-stop-server.py

or, when using a specific configuration:

python3 MTUOC-stop-server.py config-server-opusmt-eng-spa.yaml

A complete engine can be downloaded and configured using MTUOC recipes. Available recipes can be found in the MTUOC-recipes repository.

You can download a recipe in two ways.

If you already have the recipe as a file:

python3 MTUOC-downloader.py recipeAina-cat-eng.yaml

Alternatively, you can provide the direct link to the recipe:

python3 MTUOC-downloader.py https://huggingface.co/datasets/aoliverg/MTUOC-recipes/resolve/main/recipeAina-cat-eng.yaml

docs.title: 1.4.3. Using the MTUOC-Server Manager
docs.text:
A graphical user interface (GUI), MTUOC-server-manager.py, is provided to simplify the process of starting, stopping, testing, and configuring MTUOC servers.

When you start the application, the following interface is displayed:

The application is organized into five tabs:

  • Control: Select an engine through its configuration file, start and stop the server, and check its status.
  • Test: Send sentences to the active server for translation.
  • Configuration Editor: Edit the basic configuration of the translation engine.
  • Aux. Editor: Edit additional configuration files required by some models.
  • Recipes: Download complete pre-configured engines from MTUOC recipes.

docs.title: The Control Tab
docs.text:
In this tab, you can select one of the available server configuration files. These files should be placed in the same directory as MTUOC-server-manager. Once you have selected a configuration, click Start to launch the server.

The console displays relevant information about the running server. Use the Stop button when you want to stop it.

docs.title: The Test Tab
docs.text: In the Test tab, you can write or paste sentences or paragraphs and send them to the active translation system. This provides a simple way to verify that the selected engine is running correctly and inspect its translations.

docs.title: The Configuration Editor Tab
docs.text:
When you click LOAD SELECTED CONFIGURATION & LINKED MODEL CONFIG, the configuration files are loaded into two tabs: 1. Server Configuration (Main) and 2. Model Configuration (Linked).

You can inspect and modify the configuration files and save your changes using the corresponding SAVE button at the bottom of the interface.

Note that changes are not applied to a running server. You must stop and restart the server for the new configuration to take effect.

docs.title: The Aux. Editor Tab
docs.text: The Aux. Editor tab allows you to edit additional text-based configuration files required by some models. You can open a file using the OPEN button, modify it, and save the resulting file using SAVE AS.

docs.title: The Recipes Tab
docs.text:
The Recipes tab allows you to download complete engines, including models, alignment models, truecasers, and other required components, from a Hugging Face repository containing MTUOC recipes.

By default, the aoliverg/MTUOC-recipes repository is selected. If you change the repository, use the CONNECT/REFRESH button to update the list of available recipes.

You can filter the available recipes by entering a search string. Once you have identified the recipe you want to use, select it and click DOWNLOAD SELECTED RECIPE.

Key Takeaways

After completing this section, you should remember that:

  • MTUOC is an open-source ecosystem for training, deploying, and integrating machine translation systems and LLMs.

  • MTUOC-server bridges translation engines and client applications, managing preprocessing, inference, postprocessing, and communication.

  • Its support for different NMT systems, LLMs, protocols, tag restoration, and translation memories facilitates integration into professional translation workflows.

  • MTUOC-server can be run and managed locally using the command line or graphical interface, while MTUOC recipes simplify the installation of complete translation engines.

docs.title: 2. Open Neural Machine Translation Models
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this section, you should be able to:

  • Understand the distinction between an NMT model and MTUOC-server and their respective roles in the translation workflow.

  • Identify the main characteristics of OpusMT and NLLB and select appropriate models and translation directions.

  • Test open NMT models independently using Python and Hugging Face.

  • Configure, run, and test OpusMT and NLLB models with MTUOC-server.

Suggested Reading

To gain a deeper understanding of the two open NMT approaches explored in this section, we recommend the following academic papers:

  • Tiedemann, J., Aulamo, M., Bakshandaeva, D., Boggia, M., Grönroos, S. A., Nieminen, T., et al. (2024). Democratizing neural machine translation with OPUS-MT. Language Resources and Evaluation, 58(2), 713–755.

Full article

  • NLLB Team (2024). Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages. Nature, 630, 841–846.

Full article

docs.title: 2.0. Overview of Open NMT Models
docs.text:
As explained in Section 1, MTUOC-server provides the infrastructure required to connect translation engines with client applications such as CAT tools and translation software. The actual translation, however, is performed by the underlying machine translation model selected in the server configuration.

When MTUOC-server is launched, it starts a specific translation engine according to the configuration file being used. The basic server configuration identifies, among other parameters:

  • the MT engine to be used;
  • the model configuration file associated with that engine;
  • the port through which client applications connect to the server;
  • the communication protocol used by the server.

For example, the default configuration distributed with MTUOC-server uses an OpusMT English–Spanish model. When the server starts, it displays information about the active model, IP address, port, and server type. Client applications need this connection information in order to send source segments to the server and receive their translations.

MTUOC-server supports different types of translation technology, including neural machine translation systems, Large Language Models (LLMs), commercial translation APIs, and rule-based machine translation systems. In this section, however, we focus specifically on two open neural machine translation model families:

  • OpusMT, a large collection of pre-trained bilingual and multilingual translation models closely associated with the OPUS parallel corpus ecosystem.
  • NLLB (No Language Left Behind), a multilingual neural machine translation system designed to support translation across more than 200 languages.

These two model families illustrate two different approaches to open NMT. OpusMT provides a large collection of models, many of which are designed for specific language pairs, whereas NLLB uses a multilingual model capable of handling a large number of source and target languages through language codes.

For both OpusMT and NLLB, we will follow a similar practical workflow:

  1. identify and select an appropriate pre-trained model;
  2. test the model independently using Python and the Hugging Face transformers library;
  3. configure the model for use with MTUOC-server;
  4. start the server and test the translation service;
  5. examine the main configuration parameters that control model behaviour.

This workflow makes it possible to distinguish clearly between the translation model, which generates the translation, and MTUOC-server, which manages deployment, communication, preprocessing, postprocessing, and integration with external applications.

Later sections will apply a similar deployment logic to Large Language Models, including models accessed through Hugging Face and other frameworks.

docs.title: 2.1. OpusMT
docs.text:
OpusMT is a project closely associated with the OPUS corpora, dedicated to the distribution of a large collection of open Neural Machine Translation models.

Many OpusMT models are designed for particular language pairs, although multilingual models are also available. The models can be downloaded from Hugging Face and deployed locally through MTUOC-server.

A large collection of available OpusMT models can be explored in the OpusMT model registry.

docs.title: 2.1.1. Testing OpusMT with Python
docs.text:
Before integrating a model into MTUOC-server, it is useful to test it independently. This allows us to verify that the model can be loaded and produces translations before introducing the server configuration.

The example script is available as translateOpusMT.py.

First, install the required Python libraries:

transformers
torch
sentencepiece
sacremoses

The following script loads an English–Spanish OpusMT model and translates a sentence:

from transformers import MarianMTModel, MarianTokenizer

def translate_text(text, model_name):
    """
    Translates a given string using a specific Opus-MT model.
    """

    # 1. Load the tokenizer and the model from Hugging Face
    tokenizer = MarianTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model = MarianMTModel.from_pretrained(model_name)

    # 2. Tokenize the input text
    # The 'pt' return_tensors means we are using PyTorch
    inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)

    # 3. Generate the translated tokens
    translated_tokens = model.generate(**inputs)

    # 4. Decode the tokens back into a human-readable string
    result = tokenizer.decode(
        translated_tokens[0],
        skip_special_tokens=True
    )

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":

    # Configuration

    # This way the model is automatically downloaded:
    # model_id = "Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-es"

    # To use an already downloaded model:
    model_id = "../../models/opus-mt-en-es"

    input_sentence = "This is a translation test using OpusMT"

    print("Loading model and performing translation...")

    # Execution
    translation = translate_text(input_sentence, model_id)

    # Output
    print("-" * 30)
    print(f"Original text:    {input_sentence}")
    print(f"Translated text:  {translation}")
    print("-" * 30)

The important distinction here is between:

model_id = "Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-es"

which downloads the model from Hugging Face when required, and:

model_id = "../../models/opus-mt-en-es"

which loads a model that has already been downloaded locally.

Try changing the input sentence and running the script again.

You can also select another OpusMT model and observe how model selection determines the available translation direction.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Configuring MTUOC-server for OpusMT
docs.text:
Once the model has been tested independently, we can make it available as a translation service through MTUOC-server.

Two configuration files are required:

config-server-opusmt.yaml
config-model-opusmt-eng-spa.yaml

The first configures MTUOC-server, while the second configures the OpusMT model.

This separation is important:

server configuration
        ↓
model configuration
        ↓
translation model

docs.title: Server configuration
docs.text:
In config-server-opusmt.yaml, set the MT engine to OpusMT and indicate the model configuration file:

MTengine: OpusMT
# OpusMT, NLLB, HuggingFace, Ollama, ctranslate2,
# GoogleT, DeepL, Marian, Eole, Apertium...
system_name: OpusMT-eng-spa
model_config: config-model-opusmt-eng-spa.yaml

The rest of the configuration controls the server itself and optional processing components:

MTUOCServer:
  port: 8000
  type: MTUOC
  # one of MTUOC, Moses, ModernMT, OpenNMT, NMTWizard
  verbosity_level: 1
  log_file: log.log

dopreprocess: False
preprocess_config: None

dotokenization: False
tokenization_config: None

dopostprocess: False
postprocess_config: None

TranslationMemory:
  use: False
  memo: None
  minsim: 100

Here, for example:

  • port specifies the port through which clients will communicate with MTUOC-server;
  • type specifies the communication protocol;
  • preprocessing and postprocessing are disabled;
  • translation memory integration is disabled.

docs.title: 2.1.3. Configuring the OpusMT Model
docs.text:
The model itself is configured in config-model-opusmt-eng-spa.yaml:

OpusMT:
  # model_path: Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-es
  model_path: "./opus-mt-en-es"
  beam_size: 5
  num_hypotheses: 5
  multilingual_prefix: ""
  device: cuda
  # cuda or cpu

The model_path parameter identifies the model to use.

You can specify a Hugging Face model:

model_path: Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-es

In this case, the model will be downloaded when required.

Alternatively, you can provide the path to a model already stored locally:

model_path: "./opus-mt-en-es"

Most OpusMT models are bilingual, meaning that the model is designed for a particular source and target language. For these models:

multilingual_prefix: ""

Some OpusMT models are multilingual. In these cases, multilingual_prefix can be used to specify the target language using the format:

>>id<<

For example:

>>ca<<

can be used when Catalan is a valid target language for the selected multilingual model.

The parameters:

beam_size: 5
num_hypotheses: 5

control aspects of translation generation and the number of translation candidates considered or produced.

Finally:

device: cuda

specifies the device on which the model will run. It can be changed to:

device: cpu

when GPU execution is not available.

docs.title: 2.1.4. Installing the OpusMT Requirements
docs.text:
If you only plan to use OpusMT, you do not necessarily need to install every dependency supported by MTUOC-server. The OpusMT-specific requirements include:

# GENERAL
pyyaml
requests
flask
waitress
websocket-client
sentencepiece
sacremoses
ftfy
protobuf

# OPUS MT
torch

docs.title: 2.1.5. Starting and Testing the Server
docs.text:
MTUOC-server can be started from the terminal:

python3 MTUOC-server.py config-server-opusmt.yaml

When the model has been successfully loaded, the terminal displays information about the running server, including the model, IP address, port, and protocol.

MTUOC server port: 8000
MTUOC server type: MTUOC

Alternatively, you can start the server using MTUOC-server-manager. Select the appropriate model in the Control tab and click Start.

If the server was started from the terminal, you can test it with:

python3 MTUOC-test-server.py config-server-opusmt.yaml

The test application allows you to enter a source text and send it to the running server.

If you are using MTUOC-server-manager, the same operation can be performed from the Test tab.

When you have finished working with the server, stop it from MTUOC-server-manager using the Stop button or from the terminal with:

python3 MTUOC-stop-server.py config-server-opusmt.yaml

docs.title: 2.1.6. Using an MTUOC Recipe
docs.text:
MTUOC recipes provide ready-made configurations that can be downloaded and adapted.

For a basic English–Spanish OpusMT configuration without preprocessing or postprocessing, you can use:

recipe-OpusMT-noprepost-eng-spa.yaml

The recipe can be installed with MTUOC-downloader:

python3 MTUOC-downloader.py https://huggingface.co/datasets/aoliverg/MTUOC-recipes/resolve/main/recipe-OpusMT-noprepost-eng-spa.yaml

Alternatively, use the Recipes tab in MTUOC-server-manager.

The downloaded recipe may place some configuration files in the MTUOC-server directory and others in the model directory.

docs.title: 2.1.7. Practical Activity
docs.text:
1. Select an OpusMT model.
  2. Test it independently using the Python script.
  3. Configure the model in MTUOC-server.
  4. Start the server.
  5. Translate several sentences using the test application.
  6. Change at least one configuration parameter and observe the result.
  7. Stop the server when you have finished.

docs.title: 2.2. NLLB
docs.text:
NLLB (No Language Left Behind) is a multilingual neural machine translation model. Unlike a bilingual model designed for one particular translation direction, the same NLLB model can translate between a large number of languages.

NLLB supports more than 200 languages. The required source and target languages are specified using language codes.

This means that changing the translation direction does not necessarily require downloading another model. Instead, the same multilingual model can be configured with different source and target language codes.

docs.title: 2.2.1. Testing NLLB with Python
docs.text:
As with OpusMT, we will first test the model independently before integrating it into MTUOC-server.

The example script is available as translateNLLB.py.

The basic requirements are:

transformers
torch

The following example uses the nllb-200-distilled-600M model:

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM

def translate_nllb(text, model_name, source_lang, target_lang):
    """
    Translates text using the NLLB model.
    """

    # 1. Load the tokenizer and model
    # NLLB uses Auto classes for easier loading
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(model_name)

    # 2. Prepare the input
    inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)

    # 3. Generate the translation specifying the target language code
    # forced_bos_token_id tells the model which language to translate into
    forced_bos_token_id = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(target_lang)

    translated_tokens = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        forced_bos_token_id=forced_bos_token_id
    )

    # 4. Decode the output
    result = tokenizer.decode(
        translated_tokens[0],
        skip_special_tokens=True
    )

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":

    # Model configuration

    # If you want to download from Hugging Face:
    # model_id = "facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M"

    # If you want to use a local version:
    model_id = "../../models/nllb-200-distilled-600M"

    # Language codes:
    # Spanish: spa_Latn | English: eng_Latn | Catalan: cat_Latn
    src_code = "eng_Latn"
    tgt_code = "spa_Latn"

    input_sentence = "This is a translated sentence using NLLB."

    print(f"Loading {model_id}...")

    translation = translate_nllb(
        input_sentence,
        model_id,
        src_code,
        tgt_code
    )

    print("-" * 30)
    print(f"Source ({src_code}): {input_sentence}")
    print(f"Target ({tgt_code}): {translation}")
    print("-" * 30)

As with OpusMT, the model can be loaded directly from Hugging Face:

model_id = "facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M"

or from a local directory:

model_id = "../../models/nllb-200-distilled-600M"

The main difference is that we also specify the language direction:

src_code = "eng_Latn"
tgt_code = "spa_Latn"

For example:

eng_Latn = English
spa_Latn = Spanish
cat_Latn = Catalan

Try changing:

tgt_code = "cat_Latn"

and translate the same English sentence into Catalan.

docs.title: 2.2.2. Configuring MTUOC-server for NLLB
docs.text:
As with OpusMT, two configuration files are required:

config-server-NLLB.yaml
config-model-NLLB.yaml

The first configures MTUOC-server and identifies NLLB as the translation engine.

A basic configuration follows the same structure used previously:

MTengine: NLLB
system_name: NLLB
model_config: config-model-NLLB.yaml

MTUOCServer:
  port: 8000
  type: MTUOC
  # one of MTUOC, Moses, ModernMT, OpenNMT, NMTWizard
  verbosity_level: 1
  log_file: log.log

dopreprocess: False
preprocess_config: None

dotokenization: False
tokenization_config: None

dopostprocess: False
postprocess_config: None

TranslationMemory:
  Path: None
  sl: es
  tl: en

The server configuration therefore identifies which engine is being used, while the model configuration specifies which NLLB model and language direction should be loaded.

docs.title: 2.2.3. Configuring the NLLB Model
docs.text:
The model configuration is stored in config-model-NLLB.yaml:

NLLB:
  # model: facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M
  model: "./nllb-200-distilled-600M"
  # A Hugging Face repository or a full/relative path to a local model
  src_lang: eng_Latn
  tgt_lang: spa_Latn
  device: gpu
  beam_size: 5
  num_hypotheses: 5

NLLB is distributed in several model sizes:

facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M
facebook/nllb-200-1.3B
facebook/nllb-200-distilled-1.3B
facebook/nllb-200-3.3B

The model parameter can point either to a Hugging Face repository:

model: facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M

or to a model already stored locally:

model: "./nllb-200-distilled-600M"

The translation direction is controlled by:

src_lang: eng_Latn
tgt_lang: spa_Latn

For example, changing the target language to Catalan requires:

src_lang: eng_Latn
tgt_lang: cat_Latn

The device parameter determines whether the model is run on the CPU or GPU:

device: gpu

The parameters:

beam_size: 5
num_hypotheses: 5

control aspects of translation generation and the number of translation candidates considered or produced.

docs.title: 2.2.4. NLLB Language Codes
docs.text:
NLLB uses language codes that identify both the language and, where relevant, the writing system.

Some useful examples are:

Language NLLB code Catalan cat_Latn Chinese (Simplified) zho_Hans Chinese (Traditional) zho_Hant English eng_Latn French fra_Latn German deu_Latn Italian ita_Latn Portuguese por_Latn Spanish spa_Latn

The appropriate codes must be used in the model configuration when defining the source and target languages.

docs.title: 2.2.5. Starting and Testing the Server
docs.text:
Once the NLLB server and model configuration files have been prepared, start MTUOC-server using the NLLB server configuration.

You can then use the MTUOC test application to send source segments to the running server and verify that the selected NLLB model and language direction are working correctly.

As with OpusMT, you can also start and test the server through MTUOC-server-manager.

When testing different translation directions, modify the source and target language codes in the NLLB model configuration and restart the server before testing the new configuration.

docs.title: 2.2.6. Practical Activity
docs.text:
1. Load facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M or the corresponding local model.
  2. Test an English–Spanish translation with the Python script.
  3. Change the target language from Spanish (spa_Latn) to Catalan (cat_Latn).
  4. Compare the two translations.
  5. Configure NLLB in MTUOC-server.
  6. Start the server and test the translation service.
  7. Change the source or target language in the model configuration and test another translation direction.

Key Takeaways

After completing this section, you should remember that:

  • The translation model and MTUOC-server have different roles: the model generates translations, while MTUOC-server deploys it and connects it with external applications.

  • OpusMT and NLLB represent different approaches to open NMT: OpusMT provides many models for specific language pairs as well as some multilingual models, while NLLB provides multilingual models supporting more than 200 languages.

  • Open NMT models can be loaded from Hugging Face or locally, tested independently, and then integrated into MTUOC-server through separate server and model configurations.

  • Once configured in MTUOC-server, NMT models can be run as translation services and subsequently integrated into professional translation workflows, including CAT tools.

docs.text: Opus-MT is a project closely associated with the OPUS corpora, dedicated to the distribution of a vast collection of open-source Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models. These models are fully compatible and can be deployed directly via the MTUOC-server.

docs.title: Testing OpusMT in a Pyhton script
docs.text:
We can use a simple python script (translateOpusMT.py to test OpusMT models. Before using the script, don't forget to install the requirements.txt:

transformers
torch
sentencepiece
sacremoses

The script is the following. Feel free to change the model to test and the sentence to translate.

from transformers import MarianMTModel, MarianTokenizer

def translate_text(text, model_name):
    """
    Translates a given string using a specific Opus-MT model.
    """
    # 1. Load the tokenizer and the model from Hugging Face
    tokenizer = MarianTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model = MarianMTModel.from_pretrained(model_name)

    # 2. Tokenize the input text
    # The 'pt' return_tensors means we are using PyTorch
    inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)

    # 3. Generate the translated tokens
    translated_tokens = model.generate(**inputs)

    # 4. Decode the tokens back into a human-readable string
    result = tokenizer.decode(translated_tokens[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Configuration
    #This way the model is automatically downloaded
    #model_id = "Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-es"
    #To use an already downloaded model
    model_id = "../../models/opus-mt-en-es"
    input_sentence = "This is a translation test using OpusMT"

    print("Loading model and performing translation...")

    # Execution
    translation = translate_text(input_sentence, model_id)

    # Output
    print("-" * 30)
    print(f"Original text:    {input_sentence}")
    print(f"Translated text:  {translation}")
    print("-" * 30)

As we don't want to translate isolated sentences one by one, the use of MTUOC-server to start a OpusMT model is very handy and the server adds several additional features.

docs.title: 2. Starting OpusMT in MTUOC-server
docs.text:
To start the MTUOC-server using a model from OpusMT we need to configure 2 files:

config-server-opusmt.yaml

We simply need to set the MTEngine field to OpusMT and state the path and name of the config file for the OpusMT model. We can also set a system_name, but this is not compulsory.

MTengine: OpusMT
#OpusMT, NLLB, HuggingFace, Ollama, ctranslate2, GoogleT, DeepL, Marian, Eole, Apertium...
system_name: OpusMT-eng-spa
model_config: config-model-opusmt-eng-spa.yaml

The rest of the configuration file is used to set the port, type of server, preprocessing, postprocessing and translation memory.

MTUOCServer:
  port: 8000
  type: MTUOC
  #one of MTUOC, Moses, ModernMT, OpenNMT, NMTWizard
  verbosity_level: 1
  #specific configuration when acting as ONMT server
  log_file: log.log

dopreprocess: False
preprocess_config: None
dotokenization: False
tokenization_config: None
dopostprocess: False
postprocess_config: None

TranslationMemory: 
  use: False
  memo: None
  minsim: 100

And then configure the model with the config-OpusMT.yaml file:

OpusMT:
  #model_path: Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-es
  model_path: "./opus-mt-en-es"
  beam_size: 5
  num_hypotheses: 5
  multilingual_prefix: ""
  device: cuda
  #cuda cpu

In model_path we need to state the model we want to use. You can see the full list of models here. We can set the model_path as model_path: Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-es and then the first time we use the model it will be automatically downloaded from HuggingFace. We can also set as a path to a model already downloaded in our system, as in model_path: "./opus-mt-en-es". Most of the models are bilingual, that is, they can translate from one source language to one target language. For bilingual models we state multilingual_prefix: "", that is, no multilingual prefix. In OpusMT, however, some models are multilingual, meaning that they can translate from and to several languages. In this case we use the multilingual_prefix in the form of >>id<< (where id is a valid target language ID of the model.) For example, >>ca<< to translate to Catalan.

The parameters beam_size and num_hypotheses are related to the number of translation candidates the model will provide for each source sentence.

You may need to install the requirements. If you plan to use only OpusMT you don't need to install the whole set of requirements for MTUOC-server, but the specific ones that are in the requirements-OpusMT.txt file. The requirements are:

#GENERAL
pyyaml
requests
flask
waitress
websocket-client
sentencepiece
sacremoses
ftfy
protobuf

#OPUS MT
#pytorch
torch

Now you can start the MTUOC-server, either in the terminal:

python3 MTUOC-server.py config-server-opusmt.yaml

And the following information will appear in the terminal:

INFO: TransformersTranslator started (Auto-device: cuda)
Loading config inside class:  config-model-opusmt-eng-spa.yaml
INFO: Device changed to cuda (the model will be loaded here)

MTUOC server IP: 192.168.0.139
MTUOC server port: 8000
MTUOC server type: MTUOC

...or using the MTUOC-server-manager, selecting the model in the Control tab, and clicking the button Start.

To test the system, if you started the system in the terminal, you can start the program MTUOC-test-server.py with the configuration file as a parameter:

python3 MTUOC-test-server.py config-server-opusmt.yaml

the following application will appear where you can write or paste a text and click the button Translate.

Or if you started the system with MTUOC-server-manager you can go to the tab Test and write or paste a text there:

Once you finish using the server, you may want to stop the server using the Stop button in the MTUOC-server-manager or writing in the terminal:

python3 MTUOC-stop-server.py config-server-opusmt.yaml

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
NLLB (No Language Left Behind) is a multilingual neural machine translation model. This means that the same model can translate from and to many languages (in the case of the NLLB model, more than 200; the complete list of languages is provided in the appendix). The MTUOC-server can deploy this model and performs the download automatically. However, when launching the model, we must specify which language pair we require (although if we change it later, it will not be necessary to download the model again).

To learn more about this model, you can read the following article:

NLLB Team. Scaling neural machine translation to 200 languages. Nature 630, 841–846 (2024).

docs.title: Testing NLLB in a Pyhton script
docs.text:
As we did with OpusMT, we can use a script to test a NLLB model. You can change the size of the model (see below), the source and target languages (see the list of available models in Appendix 1) and the sentence to translate. The script is translateNLLB.py:

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM

def translate_nllb(text, model_name, source_lang, target_lang):
    """
    Translates text using the NLLB model.
    """
    # 1. Load the tokenizer and model
    # NLLB uses Auto classes for easier loading
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(model_name)

    # 2. Prepare the input and specify the source language
    inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)

    # 3. Generate the translation specifying the target language code
    # forced_bos_token_id tells the model which language to translate into
    forced_bos_token_id = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(target_lang)
    translated_tokens = model.generate(
        **inputs, 
        forced_bos_token_id=forced_bos_token_id
    )

    # 4. Decode the output
    result = tokenizer.decode(translated_tokens[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Model configuration
    #If you want to download from HuggingFace
    #model_id = "facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M"
    #If you want to use a local version
    model_id = "../../models/nllb-200-distilled-600M"
    # Language Codes: 
    # Spanish: spa_Latn | English: eng_Latn | Catalan: cat_Latn
    src_code = "eng_Latn" 
    tgt_code = "spa_Latn"

    input_sentence = "This is a translated sentence using NLLB."

    print(f"Loading {model_id}...")

    translation = translate_nllb(input_sentence, model_id, src_code, tgt_code)

    print("-" * 30)
    print(f"Source ({src_code}): {input_sentence}")
    print(f"Target ({tgt_code}): {translation}")
    print("-" * 30)

And the requirements.txt:

transformers
torch

config-model-NLLB.yaml

We have to configure the following parameters:

NLLB:
  #model: facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M

  src_lang: eng_Latn

  device: gpu

  • facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M

The source language code (scr_lang) and target language code (tgt_lang) should be set, following the available languages and codes on Appendix 1.

In the field device we should set whether we want to use the cpu or gpu.

docs.title: 3. Integration into CAT Tools
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this section, you should be able to:

  • Explain how MTUOC-server connects machine translation systems with professional CAT tools.

  • Install and configure the MTUOC plugins for OmegaT and RWS Trados Studio.

  • Configure and test the connection between a CAT tool and a running MTUOC-server.

  • Use machine translation suggestions from MTUOC-server within a CAT-tool workflow alongside other translation resources.

Suggested Reading

Before working through this section, you may find the following practical resources useful:

  • OmegaT for CAT Beginners. An introduction to the basic concepts and workflow of OmegaT. OmegaT for CAT Beginners

  • OmegaT User Manual – Machine Translation. Documentation on using machine translation services within OmegaT. OmegaT Manual: Machine Translation

  • RWS Trados Studio – Level 1 Course. An introduction to the Trados Studio workflow, including the use of neural machine translation providers within translation projects. Trados Studio Level 1 Course Outline

docs.title: 3.0. From MTUOC-Server to the CAT Tool
docs.text:
In the previous sections, we examined two fundamental components of the machine translation workflow. In Section 1, we introduced MTUOC-server as the middleware that manages communication between translation engines and external applications. In Section 2, we deployed open neural machine translation models such as OpusMT and NLLB through the server.

The next step is to make these translation services available within the environment where professional translators actually work: the Computer-Assisted Translation (CAT) tool.

The basic architecture can be represented as follows:

MT model → MTUOC-server → CAT tool → translator

The machine translation model generates the translation, while MTUOC-server makes the translation service accessible to the CAT tool. The translator can then receive MT suggestions directly within the translation environment, alongside other resources such as translation memories.

MTUOC provides dedicated plugins for two CAT tools covered in this section:

  • OmegaT, a free and open-source CAT tool.
  • RWS Trados Studio, a commercial CAT tool widely used in professional translation environments.

Although the installation and configuration procedures differ, the underlying principle is the same. The plugin acts as a client of MTUOC-server: it sends source segments to the server and receives the corresponding machine translations.

For this communication to work, the CAT tool needs to know where the server is running. Two parameters are particularly important:

  • IP address or server name: identifies the computer on which MTUOC-server is running.
  • Port: identifies the communication endpoint configured for that server.

If MTUOC-server and the CAT tool are running on the same computer, the connection can be entirely local. If the server is running on another computer, the plugin can connect to it using the appropriate server address and port.

Before configuring either CAT tool, make sure that the MTUOC-server you want to use is running.

docs.title: 3.1.1. OmegaT and Machine Translation
docs.text:
OmegaT is a free and open-source CAT tool. It provides support for translation memories, terminology, machine translation, and other resources used during the translation process.

This section assumes that you are already familiar with the basic OmegaT workflow. If you have not used OmegaT before, consult the OmegaT for CAT Beginners resource listed under Suggested Reading before continuing.

MTUOC-server can be integrated into OmegaT through the MTUOC MT Engine plugin. Once configured, translations generated by MTUOC-server become available directly in OmegaT's Machine Translation pane.

docs.title: 3.1.2. Installing the MTUOC Plugin
docs.text:
Download the MTUOC plugin:

MtuocTranslatePlugin-0.1.0.jar

Place the downloaded JAR file in the appropriate OmegaT plugin directory for your operating system:

  • Windows: C:\Program Files\OmegaT\plugin
  • Linux: $HOME/.omegat/plugin
  • macOS: ~/Library/Preferences/OmegaT/plugins

NOTE: These paths may vary depending on your OmegaT installation and configuration.

Once the JAR file has been copied to the appropriate directory, launch OmegaT.

docs.title: 3.1.3. Configuring the Connection
docs.text:
To configure the MTUOC plugin:

  1. Go to Options > Preferences.

  1. Select Machine Translation in the sidebar.

  2. Select MTUOC MT Engine and click Configure.

  1. Enter the connection details for the MTUOC-server you want to use. The server can be running either locally or on a remote computer.

The connection details should correspond to the IP address and port displayed when you started MTUOC-server.

docs.title: 3.1.4. Testing and Using the MT Engine
docs.text:
Once the connection details have been entered, click Test connection.

If OmegaT can communicate correctly with MTUOC-server, the following message will be displayed:

Server connection OK

The MTUOC machine translation engine is now available in OmegaT.

When you work on a translation project, source segments can be sent to MTUOC-server and the resulting translations will appear automatically in the Machine Translation pane.

The translation model used by OmegaT is determined by the MTUOC-server to which the plugin is connected. For example, if the server is running the English–Spanish OpusMT model configured in Section 2, the plugin will receive translations generated by that model.

For additional information about machine translation integration in OmegaT, consult the OmegaT User Manual.

docs.title: 3.2.1. Trados Studio and Machine Translation
docs.text:
RWS Trados Studio is a commercial CAT tool that allows translators to combine different translation resources within the same project, including translation memories and machine translation providers.

MTUOC provides a dedicated plugin that allows Trados Studio to connect to MTUOC-server and retrieve machine translation suggestions.

As with OmegaT, the plugin does not run the translation model itself. It sends source segments to the configured MTUOC-server and receives the resulting translations.

docs.title: 3.2.2. Downloading and Installing the MTUOC Plugin
docs.text:
Download the MTUOC plugin corresponding to your version of Trados Studio and unzip the downloaded file.

Before installing a new version of the MTUOC plugin, uninstall any previous version that may already be installed.

Open the uncompressed folder and double-click the plugin installation file:

The installation interface will appear:

Select the appropriate version of Trados Studio and choose where the plugin should be installed. Then click Next and complete the installation.

docs.title: Unsigned Plugin Warning
docs.text:
Depending on the plugin version, Trados Studio may display a warning indicating that the plugin is unsigned:

If you are installing the MTUOC plugin obtained from the official MTUOC distribution, click Yes to continue.

Some newly released versions of the plugin may temporarily be unsigned while the corresponding signing process is being completed.

docs.title: 3.2.3. Configuring the Connection
docs.text:
Open a Trados Studio project and go to Project Settings.

Select Translation Memory and Automated Translation for either all language pairs or the specific language pair you want to configure.

Select MTUOC-MACHINE TRANSLATION as a translation provider.

Open Settings to access the MTUOC plugin configuration.

The configuration interface contains three main tabs:

  • General
  • Connection test
  • Advanced

docs.title: General Tab
docs.text:
The General tab contains the basic connection parameters.

Enter:

  • the IP address or server name of the MTUOC-server;
  • the port used by that server.

The language pair is not specified in the plugin itself. Each IP address and port combination connects to a particular running MTUOC-server configuration, and the plugin does not verify whether the language pair used by the server corresponds to the language pair of the Trados project.

You should therefore make sure that the MTUOC-server configuration corresponds to the translation direction required by your project.

docs.title: 3.2.4. Testing the Connection
docs.text:
Before using the server in your project, open the Connection test tab:

Enter or paste a source sentence and click Send.

This test allows you to verify that:

  1. Trados can connect to the specified IP address and port;
  2. MTUOC-server is running;
  3. the server can process the request and return a translation.

Testing the connection before beginning a translation project can help distinguish connection problems from problems related to the CAT-tool project itself.

docs.title: 3.2.5. Advanced Settings
docs.text: The Advanced tab provides additional options for integrating machine translation into the Trados workflow.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
The Keep the cache (days) setting determines how long translations retrieved from MTUOC-server are stored in the plugin cache.

The cache can also be cleared manually using the Delete cache button.

docs.title: Translation Score
docs.text:
The Score setting assigns a score to machine translation results.

This is particularly relevant when machine translation is used alongside a translation memory. The score allows the MT result to be compared with translation memory matches so that the different translation resources can be combined within the same workflow.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The Description setting determines how translations produced through the MTUOC plugin are identified in the project's SDLXLIFF file.

Available values include:

Unknown
TM
Machine translation
Alignment
Context TM
Adaptative Machine Translation
Nmt
AutomaticTranslation

These settings allow machine translation output to be identified and managed as part of the wider Trados project workflow.

docs.title: 3.2.6. Using MTUOC-Server in a Trados Project
docs.text:
Once the plugin has been configured and the connection tested, activate the MTUOC translation provider in the project. Source segments can then be sent to the configured MTUOC-server, and the returned translations become available alongside the other translation resources in Trados Studio.

If you want to change the underlying translation model — for example, from an OpusMT model to an NLLB model — the change takes place on the MTUOC-server side. The CAT tool continues to communicate with MTUOC-server through the configured IP address and port.

NOTE: If you experience problems installing, updating, or uninstalling the MTUOC plugin, consult the Troubleshooting section of the course.

Key Takeaways

After completing this section, you should remember that:

  • MTUOC-server acts as a bridge between translation models and professional CAT tools, while the CAT tool itself does not run the translation model.

  • OmegaT and RWS Trados Studio can connect to MTUOC-server through dedicated plugins using the server IP address and port.

  • Once connected, machine translation suggestions can be incorporated into the CAT-tool workflow alongside other resources such as translation memories.

  • The translation model remains separate from the CAT tool: models can be changed on the MTUOC-server side without changing the basic CAT-tool integration architecture.

docs.title: 1. Installation
docs.text:
• Download the plugin: MtuocTranslatePlugin-0.1.0.jar.

  • Place the JAR file in the corresponding directory for your operating system:

  • Windows: C:\Program Files\OmegaT\plugin

  • Linux: $HOME/.omegat/plugin
  • Mac: ~/Library/Preferences/OmegaT/plugins

Note: These paths may vary depending on your specific OmegaT installation and configuration.

docs.title: 2. Plugin configuration
docs.text:
Once the JAR file is in the correct folder, launch OmegaT and follow these steps:

  1. Navigate to Options > Preferences.

  1. In the sidebar, select Machine Translation.

  2. Select MTUOC MT Engine and click Configure.

  1. Enter the details for your available system (either a local or remote server).

  2. Click Test connection to verify the setup. If the configuration is correct, the message "Server connection OK" will be displayed.

The MT engine is now active, and suggestions will appear automatically in the Machine Translation pane.

For further details on integration settings, please consult the OmegaT manual: Machine translations

docs.title: Downloading the plug-in
docs.text: Download the plug-in for your version of Trados Studio. At the moment we offer a plug-in for each of the following versions: 2019, 2021 and 2022. Once downloaded, unzip the file.

docs.title: Installing the plug-in
docs.text:
Uninstall any previous versions of the MTUOC Trados plugin before installing the new version. Open the uncompressed folder and doble-clic to the file:

The following interface will appear:

Choose the correct version of Trados Studio and the folder (for all the domain computers, current user or all users) where the plug-in will be installed. Clic on the Next button. Once the installation is completed click on the Finnish button.

docs.title: Unsigned plug-in warning
docs.text:
Depending on the version of the plug-in, when opening Trados Studio, a warning indicating that the plug-in is unsigned may appear. As the following one:

Answer Yes.

The plug-ins are signed by Trados and we ask for the signature once a new version of the plug-in is released. As this process takes some days, you may eventually find unsigned plug-ins.

docs.title: Plug-in configuration
docs.text:
To configure the plug-in, once opened a project go to Project Configuration and select Translation memory and machine translation, either for All language combination or for a given languae combination. Then select Use and clic on MTUOC-MACHINE TRANSLATION and this plug-in will appear:

Unselect it, in case it's selected, and then clic on Settings. The following interface will appear:

docs.title: General tab
docs.text: In this tab we can set the IP (or server name) and Port of the MTUOC server. No language pair is provided as each IP and port serves an unique language pair. The plug-in, nor Trados, make no language verification, so the user should know the language pair of the IP and port combination.

docs.title: Connection test tab
docs.text: In this tab we can perform a connection test to make sure the server works properly. Write or paste a source sentence and clic on the button Send

docs.title: Advanced tab
docs.text:
In this tab some advanced configuration can be set:

  • Cache - Keep the cache (days): to set how many days the cache sould be kept. You can also delete the cache at any moment clicking on the Delete cache button.
  • Translation configuration:
  • Score: the score given to the machine translation. This allows to combine machine translation with translation memories. The machine translation target will be selected of the best translation memory match is under this score.
  • Description: the description string that will be set in the SDLXLIFF file of the project for the translated segments coming from machine translation. The following values can be set: Unknown, TM, Machine translation, Alignment, Context TM, Adaptative Machine Translation, Nmt and AutomaticTranslation.

To accept the configuration the button Accept can be clicked in any tab.

To close and accept the project settings click on the button OK.

Once the configuration is done, the source segments will be translated with the MTUOC server set in the configuration.

docs.title: Using the Plugin Installer
docs.text:
Your Trados Studio distribution comes with a program that facilitates the installation and uninstallation of plugins. The program is called Sdl.Community.SdlPluginInstaller.exe. Depending on the version this program can be located in different folders on your computer.

In this interface, be sure the correct version of Trados is selected in Filter by Studio version:". The plugin will appear and you can uninstall it clicking on the Uninstall** button at the right of the plugin.

For other versions of Trados Studio, for example the 2021, the program can be located at: Program Files (x86)> SDL > Plugin installer.

docs.title: Manually uninstalling the plugin
docs.text:
You can also manually uninstall the plugin deleting some files and folders in your computer. The location of these files and foldes may depend on the version and the installation.

Under this folder, you'll find two subfolders: Packages and Unpacked. In the Unpacked folder, delete the SDL.Trados.MTUOC folder. If this plugin is the only one installed in the system, you can safely delete all the Unpacked folder. Then, go to the Packages folder and delete all the files and folders corresponding to this plugin.

The plugin can manually installed following these steps:
