docs.title: 4. Large Language Models and Translation
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this section, you should be able to:

  • Explain how LLM-based translation differs from conventional NMT and distinguish between general-purpose and translation-specific LLMs.

  • Identify the main factors involved in selecting an LLM for translation, including language coverage, model purpose, computational requirements, and licence.

  • Design translation prompts incorporating relevant context, terminology, examples, constraints, and output requirements.

  • Understand how LLMs can be used for translation and related tasks and how open models can be deployed locally within a translation workflow.

Suggested Reading

To gain a deeper understanding of the use of Large Language Models for machine translation, we recommend the following resources:

  • Hendy, A. et al. (2023). How Good Are GPT Models at Machine Translation? A Comprehensive Evaluation. Read Paper on arXiv

  • Alves, D. M. et al. (2024). Tower: An Open Multilingual Large Language Model for Translation-Related Tasks. Read Paper on arXiv

  • Hugging Face. Model Cards. Documentation explaining the information provided in model cards, including model uses, limitations, training information, and evaluation. Hugging Face Model Cards

docs.title: 4.0. From Neural Machine Translation to Large Language Models
docs.text:
In Section 2, we worked with Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models such as OpusMT and NLLB. These models are specifically designed to translate text from one language into another. Given a source text and the appropriate source and target language settings, the model generates a translation.

Large Language Models (LLMs) represent a different approach. Rather than being designed exclusively for translation, general-purpose LLMs are trained to process and generate language and can perform a wide variety of tasks. Translation is therefore one of many possible tasks that can be carried out by the same model.

This difference can be represented in simplified form as follows:

NMT

source text → translation model → target text

LLM

instruction + source text + optional additional information → language model → generated response

The instruction is particularly important. With a conventional NMT model, the task is already defined: the system is expected to translate. With a general-purpose LLM, we normally need to tell the model what task it should perform. This is done through a prompt.

For example:

Translate the following sentence from English into Spanish:

The meeting will take place next Monday.

The same LLM could receive the same sentence with a completely different instruction:

Summarize the following sentence:

The meeting will take place next Monday.

or:

Identify the named entities in the following sentence:

The meeting will take place next Monday.

The model itself has not changed; what has changed is the task specified in the prompt.

docs.title: LLMs and the Evolution of Machine Translation
docs.text:
The use of LLMs for translation has increased rapidly in recent years. General-purpose LLMs and models specifically adapted for translation are now being explored and used as complete translation systems or as components of more complex machine translation workflows.

The distinction between NMT and LLM-based translation should therefore not be understood as a simple replacement of one technology by another. Dedicated NMT systems continue to be widely used and can offer important advantages in terms of speed, computational efficiency, predictability, and deployment. LLMs, on the other hand, introduce additional possibilities, particularly because they can use instructions and contextual information and perform multiple language-related tasks within the same model.

In the previous sections, the translation workflow was represented as:

NMT model → MTUOC-server → CAT tool → translator

The same general architecture can be used with an LLM:

LLM → MTUOC-server → CAT tool → translator

However, as we will see throughout this section, deploying an LLM for translation involves some additional decisions, particularly regarding model selection, prompts, generation parameters, and output processing.

docs.title: 4.1. Large Language Models for Translation
docs.text: Not all LLMs used for translation have been developed for the same purpose. A useful initial distinction can be made between general-purpose LLMs and translation-specific LLMs.

docs.title: 4.1.1. General-purpose LLMs
docs.text:
A general-purpose LLM is designed to perform many different language-related tasks rather than translation alone. Depending on the model and its training, these tasks may include:

  • text generation;
  • question answering;
  • summarization;
  • information extraction;
  • classification;
  • rewriting and correction;
  • programming;
  • translation.

Many models are also instruction-tuned, meaning that they have been trained to respond to instructions formulated by users. This makes it possible to specify a translation task through natural-language prompts.

For example:

Translate the following text from English into Catalan:

Machine translation systems are increasingly integrated into professional translation workflows.

The main advantage of this approach is flexibility. The prompt can contain considerably more information than the source sentence alone. For example, we can tell the model who the intended reader is, specify the domain of the document, provide terminology, indicate the desired register, or supply examples of previous translations.

A general-purpose model can also be used for several stages of the same workflow. The same model could first translate a text, then revise a translation, identify terminology, or perform other language-processing tasks.

This flexibility also introduces an important difference from dedicated NMT. Since a general-purpose LLM is not exclusively a translation engine, its behaviour depends strongly on the instructions it receives. The model may also generate explanations, comments, alternative translations, or other text that was not explicitly requested. Controlling the prompt and the format of the output therefore becomes particularly important when LLMs are incorporated into automated translation workflows.

docs.title: 4.1.2. Translation-specific LLMs
docs.text:
Other LLMs have been trained or fine-tuned specifically for machine translation. These models retain the general architecture of an LLM but have been adapted so that translation becomes one of their main functions.

Examples include models such as TowerInstruct and SalamandraTA.

Translation-specific LLMs may differ from general-purpose models in several respects:

  • the training or fine-tuning data may contain substantial amounts of parallel or translation-oriented data;
  • the model may support a defined set of translation directions;
  • it may expect instructions to follow a particular format;
  • it may have been optimised specifically for translation quality or translation-related tasks.

An important practical consequence is that we should not assume that the same prompt is appropriate for every LLM.

For example, a general-purpose instruction model may respond well to a natural-language instruction such as:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish:

A translation-specific model may recommend a different prompt structure or a specific set of language identifiers. The appropriate format is normally documented in the model's model card.

docs.title: 4.1.3. Model Cards
docs.text:
Open models distributed through repositories such as Hugging Face normally include a model card. Before downloading or using an LLM for translation, it is important to consult this documentation.

A model card may provide information about:

  • the purpose of the model;
  • the base model from which it was derived;
  • supported languages;
  • training or fine-tuning data;
  • recommended tasks;
  • prompt or chat templates;
  • model size and available variants;
  • hardware or software requirements;
  • licence conditions;
  • known limitations.

This information is particularly important for translation. The fact that an LLM is multilingual does not necessarily mean that all its languages or translation directions are equally well supported.

Similarly, the ability of an LLM to translate a language pair that was not explicitly included as a translation direction during fine-tuning does not guarantee that the resulting translation will be of sufficient quality. LLMs may exhibit zero-shot translation capabilities, that is, the ability to perform translation in language combinations or settings for which they were not explicitly trained, but performance needs to be evaluated for the intended use case.

docs.title: 4.1.4. Selecting an LLM for Translation
docs.text:
Before using an LLM as a translation system, several factors should be considered:

  • Model purpose: Is the model a general-purpose instruction model or has it been specifically optimised for translation?

  • Supported languages: Does the model explicitly support the source and target languages required for the project?

  • Model size: How large is the model, and can it be run with the available computational resources?

  • Prompt format: Does the model use ordinary natural-language instructions, a predefined translation template, or a specific chat format?

  • Licence: Under what conditions can the model be used, particularly in professional or commercial applications?

  • Computational requirements: Can the model be deployed efficiently on the available hardware?

  • Translation performance: Does the model provide adequate quality for the relevant language pair, domain, and type of text?

The choice of an LLM is therefore not simply a question of selecting the largest or most recent model. It involves finding a suitable balance between translation capabilities, language coverage, computational requirements, controllability, and the intended translation scenario.

In the following section, we will focus on one of the most distinctive aspects of LLM-based translation: prompting.

docs.title: 4.2. Prompting LLMs for Translation
docs.text:
When using a conventional NMT system, the input normally consists of the source text to be translated, together with information specifying the source and target languages when required by the model. With an LLM, the input can contain much more information.

A prompt is the instruction and information provided to the model to specify what it should do. For translation, a prompt may include not only the source text and the translation direction, but also information about the domain, intended audience, terminology, style, context, or desired output format.

Prompt design is therefore an important component of LLM-based translation. Different prompts applied to the same source text and the same model may produce different translations.

docs.title: 4.2.1. Basic Translation Prompts
docs.text:
For a general-purpose instruction-tuned LLM, a translation request can be expressed using a simple natural-language instruction:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish:

This software can be installed on Windows, Linux and macOS.

The instruction explicitly identifies:

  • the task: translation;
  • the source language: English;
  • the target language: Spanish;
  • the source text to be translated.

In many cases, this is sufficient to obtain a translation. However, general-purpose LLMs may return additional information, such as an introductory sentence, comments, explanations, or alternative translations.

For use in an automated translation workflow, we generally want the model to return only the translated text. The instruction can therefore be made more explicit:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish.
Return only the translation and do not add any explanations or comments.

This software can be installed on Windows, Linux and macOS.

Translation-specific LLMs may use different instructions. Some have been fine-tuned with a particular prompt template and are expected to receive requests in that format.

For this reason, before designing a prompt, always check the model card to determine whether the developers recommend a specific prompt or chat template.

docs.title: 4.2.2. Adding Context and Translation Instructions
docs.text:
One of the main advantages of LLM-based translation is the possibility of incorporating additional information directly into the prompt.

Consider a simple translation instruction:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish:

The mouse is not working properly.

Without further information, the model has to infer the meaning of mouse from the sentence itself. We can reduce this ambiguity by providing contextual information:

You are translating the user manual of a computer peripheral from English into Spanish.

Translate the following text:

The mouse is not working properly.

Return only the Spanish translation.

Context can be provided at different levels. A translation prompt may specify, for example:

  • the domain of the text;
  • the text type or genre;
  • the communicative situation;
  • the intended audience;
  • the purpose of the translation;
  • the desired style or register;
  • information from the surrounding text.

The prompt can also assign a role to the model:

You are a professional translator specialising in medical translation.

Translate the following text from English into Spanish.
Use appropriate medical terminology and maintain a formal register.

[source text]

Role instructions are not a substitute for relevant contextual or terminological information, but they can form part of a more detailed set of translation instructions.

The amount of information included in the prompt should be appropriate to the task. Adding more instructions does not automatically produce a better translation. Instructions should be relevant, clear, and consistent.

docs.title: 4.2.3. Terminology and Glossaries
docs.text:
Terminology can also be incorporated directly into a translation prompt. This is particularly useful when a project requires specific translations for specialised terms, product names, institutional terminology, or other expressions.

For example:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish.

Use the following terminology:
machine translation = traducción automática
translation memory = memoria de traducción
language model = modelo de lenguaje

Return only the translation.

[source text]

The glossary becomes part of the information available to the model when generating the translation.

This approach can be useful for:

  • maintaining preferred terminology;
  • adapting translations to a particular client or organisation;
  • improving consistency;
  • preventing unwanted translations of product names or other expressions.

Terminological instructions can also be formulated as explicit constraints:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish.

Always translate "machine translation" as "traducción automática".
Do not translate "MTUOC-server".

Return only the translation.

[source text]

However, terminology provided through a prompt is an instruction rather than a hard constraint. An LLM may occasionally fail to apply a requested term consistently. Terminological compliance should therefore be checked when this is critical to the translation task.

docs.title: 4.2.4. Providing Translation Examples
docs.text:
Another way of guiding an LLM is to provide examples of the behaviour we expect.

A prompt containing only an instruction and the new source text is commonly referred to as zero-shot prompting: the model is asked to perform the task without being given examples within the prompt.

If one or more examples are provided before the new input, we can use few-shot prompting.

For example:

Translate from English into Spanish following the style of these examples.

English: Click Save to continue.
Spanish: Haga clic en Guardar para continuar.

English: Select the file you want to open.
Spanish: Seleccione el archivo que desea abrir.

English: Restart the application after installation.
Spanish:

The previous translations provide the model with information about the expected terminology, register, and style.

Examples can be particularly useful when:

  • a specific translation style must be reproduced;
  • previous approved translations are available;
  • the desired behaviour is difficult to describe through rules alone;
  • consistency with existing translations is important.

Examples should be carefully selected. Incorrect, inconsistent, or irrelevant examples may guide the model in the wrong direction.

docs.title: 4.2.5. Positive and Negative Constraints
docs.text:
Prompts can specify both what the model should do and what it should not do.

A positive instruction might be:

Use formal Spanish.

A negative instruction might be:

Do not translate product names.

Several constraints can be combined:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish.

Use a formal register.
Use the terminology provided in the glossary.
Do not translate product names.
Do not add explanations, notes, or alternative translations.
Return only the translated text.

[source text]

Negative constraints can be useful when a model repeatedly produces unwanted behaviour. However, prompts should remain as simple as possible. If a constraint is unnecessary, it does not need to be included.

docs.title: 4.2.6. Controlling the Output
docs.text:
Output control becomes particularly important when an LLM is connected to another application.

In an interactive chat, a response such as:

Here is the Spanish translation:

Este software puede instalarse en Windows, Linux y macOS.

may be perfectly acceptable. In a CAT-tool workflow, however, the introductory sentence is unwanted: only the translation should be inserted into the translation environment.

A prompt can explicitly request:

Return only the translation. Do not add explanations, labels, quotation marks, or comments.

Another possibility is to ask the model to place the translation between predefined delimiters:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish.

Return the translation between <translation> and </translation> tags.

[source text]

The expected response would then be:

<translation>Este software puede instalarse en Windows, Linux y macOS.</translation>

The translation can subsequently be extracted automatically from the response.

This distinction is important when moving from interactive use of an LLM to integration into a translation workflow. A response that is useful to a human user is not necessarily suitable for automatic processing.

MTUOC-server can use prompts to define the task sent to an LLM and regular expressions to extract the required translation from the generated response. We will return to this issue when configuring LLMs for MTUOC-server in Section 5.

docs.title: 4.3. LLMs for Translation-related Tasks
docs.text: Translation is not the only task that LLMs can perform within a translation workflow. Because instruction-tuned LLMs can respond to different types of prompts, the same model can potentially be used for several tasks simply by changing the instruction and the information provided to it.

docs.title: 4.3.1. Automatic Post-editing
docs.text:
An LLM can be asked to revise the output of another machine translation system. In this case, the prompt can contain both the original source text and the machine translation:

Improve the following machine translation.

Source:
[source text]

Machine translation:
[machine-translated text]

Correct translation errors while preserving the meaning of the source text.
Return only the revised translation.

This use of an LLM is generally referred to as automatic post-editing (APE).

The model is not generating a translation entirely from scratch. Instead, it receives an existing translation and is instructed to identify and correct problems in it.

docs.title: 4.3.2. Error and Grammar Correction
docs.text:
LLMs can also be instructed to correct linguistic errors without performing translation:

Correct any grammatical, spelling, and punctuation errors in the following Spanish text.
Do not change its meaning.
Return only the corrected text.

[text]

Depending on the workflow, correction can be applied to source texts, machine-translated texts, or other content.

The distinction between correction and rewriting should be made explicit in the prompt. If the model is simply asked to "improve" a text, it may make stylistic changes that go beyond error correction.

docs.title: 4.3.3. Paragraph-level and Context-aware Translation
docs.text:
Conventional translation workflows often process text segment by segment. However, individual sentences may not contain all the information needed to resolve ambiguity, maintain lexical consistency, or choose appropriate references.

LLMs can accept larger amounts of contextual information. Instead of translating an isolated sentence, we can provide a complete paragraph or additional surrounding text.

For example:

Translate the following paragraph from English into Spanish.
Take the full paragraph into account when resolving references and lexical ambiguity.
Return only the translation.

[paragraph]

Alternatively, contextual sentences can be provided while clearly identifying which segment should actually be translated:

Use the following previous sentence as context:

[previous sentence]

Translate only this sentence into Spanish:

[current sentence]

The ability to use wider context is one of the potentially important advantages of LLM-based translation. However, providing more context also increases the amount of input processed by the model and does not guarantee that the model will use all contextual information correctly.

docs.title: 4.3.4. Named Entity Recognition and Other Supporting Tasks
docs.text:
LLMs can also perform tasks that support translation without directly generating the final translation.

For example, a model can be asked to identify named entities:

Identify all person names, organisations, and locations in the following text.

Return one entity per line using this format:

entity | type

[text]

Other possible supporting tasks include terminology extraction, text classification, summarisation, and information extraction.

The important point is that an LLM can potentially perform different operations within the same translation workflow. The model remains the same; the task changes according to the prompt.

docs.title: 4.4. Running Open LLMs Locally
docs.text: LLMs can be accessed through remote services, but open models can also be downloaded and executed on local hardware. Local execution is particularly relevant to the MTUOC approach because it allows translation technologies to be integrated into professional workflows while maintaining greater control over models and data.

docs.title: 4.4.1. Remote and Local LLMs
docs.text:
A remote LLM is normally accessed through an API. The source text and instructions are sent to an external service, which runs the model and returns the generated response.

This approach has several advantages:

  • no local model installation is required;
  • the computational resources are provided by the service;
  • powerful models can be accessed from relatively modest computers.

However, it also means that data are transmitted to an external service and that access may depend on connectivity, service availability, pricing, and provider conditions.

With a locally deployed LLM, the model weights are downloaded and inference takes place on hardware controlled by the user or organisation.

Potential advantages include:

  • greater control over data;
  • the possibility of processing data without sending them to an external provider;
  • greater control over the model and its configuration;
  • independence from external API availability and pricing.

Local execution also has costs. LLMs can require substantial amounts of RAM, GPU memory, storage space, and computational power.

The choice between remote and local execution therefore depends on the translation scenario, available hardware, data requirements, and the characteristics of the model.

docs.title: 4.4.2. Finding Open LLMs
docs.text:
Many open LLMs are distributed through model repositories such as Hugging Face.

A model repository normally contains the model files together with documentation describing how the model should be used. As discussed in Section 4.1, the model card should be consulted before selecting and downloading a model.

Particular attention should be paid to:

  • supported languages;
  • intended tasks;
  • recommended prompt format;
  • model size;
  • available model variants;
  • software dependencies;
  • licence;
  • hardware requirements.

The same model family may be available in several versions. Selecting the appropriate version is therefore part of the deployment process.

docs.title: 4.4.3. Model Size and Computational Requirements
docs.text:
LLM names often include an indication of the approximate number of parameters in the model. For example, a model described as 7B contains approximately seven billion parameters.

In general, increasing the number of parameters increases the amount of memory required to load and run the model. However, model size alone does not determine translation quality: training data, model architecture, fine-tuning, supported languages, and the translation task itself are also important.

Models can also be distributed using different numerical representations. Quantisation reduces the precision used to represent model parameters, making it possible to reduce memory and storage requirements.

For example, a quantised version of a model may be substantially smaller than the original full-precision model and may therefore be usable on hardware on which the original model could not be loaded.

Quantisation involves a trade-off between:

  • memory requirements;
  • storage requirements;
  • inference speed;
  • model quality.

For the purposes of this course, the important practical point is that the same model may be available in variants with very different hardware requirements. When selecting a model for local translation, you should therefore check not only the model family and parameter count but also the specific version you intend to run.

docs.title: 4.4.4. Tools for Local LLM Execution
docs.text:
Several frameworks and applications can be used to run open LLMs locally. Some work directly with model files distributed through Hugging Face, while others simplify model downloading, quantisation formats, model loading, and inference.

Regardless of the specific framework, the basic process is similar:

  1. identify an appropriate model;
  2. check its requirements and documentation;
  3. download the required model files;
  4. load the model using a compatible framework;
  5. provide the prompt and source text;
  6. generate and process the response.

This is conceptually similar to the workflow followed with OpusMT and NLLB in Section 2, where we first identified and tested a model before deploying it through MTUOC-server.

With LLMs, however, the prompt and the processing of the generated response become additional components of the deployment configuration.

docs.title: 4.5. Preparing an LLM for a Translation Workflow
docs.text:
The general architecture introduced earlier in this section can be used to integrate LLMs into professional translation workflows. However, deploying an LLM involves several additional elements that need to be configured:

  • Model selection: choosing a model that supports the required languages and translation task.
  • Prompt definition: specifying how the translation request will be formulated.
  • Generation parameters: controlling aspects of text generation where appropriate.
  • Output format: determining how the model should return the translation.
  • Output extraction: removing any additional content and extracting the text that should be sent back to the client application.

The processing workflow can therefore be represented more explicitly as:

source segment → prompt construction → LLM → response processing → MTUOC-server → CAT tool

This is particularly important in professional translation environments. The CAT tool expects a translation for the source segment it sends to the server. Any explanations, labels, comments, or other material generated by the LLM need to be prevented through prompting or removed before the response reaches the CAT tool.

In Section 5, we will put these concepts into practice by integrating open LLMs into MTUOC-server. We will work with different types of models and examine how model-specific prompts and configuration options are incorporated into the translation workflow.

Key Takeaways

After completing this section, you should remember that:

  • LLMs provide a different approach to machine translation from conventional NMT: they can perform translation as one of many language-related tasks and may be general-purpose or specifically adapted for translation.

  • Selecting an LLM for translation requires considering its intended purpose, supported languages, translation performance, model size, computational requirements, licence, and documentation.

  • Prompting is a central component of LLM-based translation and can incorporate context, terminology, examples, constraints, and output instructions to guide translation behaviour.

  • LLMs can support translation and related tasks and can be accessed remotely or run locally; when integrated into professional workflows, prompts and generated responses must be carefully controlled and processed.

docs.title: 5. Large Language Models Integration into MTUOC-server
docs.text:
Learning Objectives

After completing this section, you should be able to:

  • Deploy and configure open LLMs locally for translation with MTUOC-server.

  • Configure prompts and generation parameters as components of an LLM-based translation system.

  • Deploy and test a translation-specific LLM with SalamandraTA and a general-purpose LLM with Gemma.

  • Compare direct local model loading through Hugging Face Transformers with model deployment through Ollama and make both types of models available to external applications through MTUOC-server.

Suggested Reading

To gain a deeper understanding of the two LLM families used in this section, we recommend the following technical and academic papers:

  • Garcia Gilabert, J., Liao, X., Da Dalt, S., Bohman, E., Mash, A., De Luca Fornaciari, F., Baucells, I., Llop, J., Claramunt, M., Escolano, C., & Melero, M. (2025). From SALAMANDRA to SALAMANDRATA: BSC Submission for WMT25 General Machine Translation Shared Task. In Proceedings of the Tenth Conference on Machine Translation, pages 614–637.

Read Paper on ACL Anthology

  • Gemma Team (2026). Gemma 4 Technical Report. arXiv:2607.02770.

Read Technical Report on arXiv

docs.title: 5.0. From LLMs to MTUOC-server
docs.text:
In Section 4, we explored how Large Language Models can be used for translation and translation-related tasks. We also saw that, unlike conventional NMT systems, LLM-based translation normally requires a prompt that tells the model what to do and may provide additional information such as context, terminology, examples, or output constraints.

We will now put these principles into practice by integrating LLMs into MTUOC-server.

The overall architecture remains the same as in the previous sections:

translation model → MTUOC-server → CAT tool → translator

However, when the translation model is an LLM, additional elements become part of the translation system:

LLM-based translation workflow through MTUOC-server.

In this section, we will work with two different models:

  • SalamandraTA, a model specifically adapted for translation and translation-related tasks;
  • Gemma, a general-purpose LLM that can be instructed to perform translation.

They also illustrate two different deployment architectures. SalamandraTA will be loaded and run locally through the Hugging Face engine, while Gemma will be managed through Ollama.

As in Section 2, we will follow a simple deployment principle:

  1. understand the model and its requirements;
  2. test it independently;
  3. configure it for MTUOC-server;
  4. start the server;
  5. test the complete translation workflow.

docs.title: 5.1. SalamandraTA
docs.text:
SalamandraTA is a family of models developed by the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC) and specifically trained for translation and translation-related tasks.

Unlike a general-purpose instruction model, SalamandraTA has been specifically trained for translation and translation-related tasks. In addition to direct translation, the model can be used for tasks such as automatic post-editing, paragraph-level translation, named entity recognition, and grammar correction.

SalamandraTA is available in different sizes, including:

salamandraTA-2b-instruct
salamandraTA-7b-instruct

In this exercise, we will use the smaller 2B instruct model, which has lower computational requirements and is therefore more suitable for local deployment.

docs.title: 5.1.1. Testing SalamandraTA with Python
docs.text:
Before integrating SalamandraTA into MTUOC-server, we will test the model independently.

SalamandraTA can be loaded directly using the Hugging Face Transformers library.

Make sure that the following Python packages are installed:

pip install torch transformers accelerate

The following script loads SalamandraTA and translates a sentence from English into Spanish:

import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

def translate_salamandra_manual(text, model_id, source_lang, target_lang):
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

    if tokenizer.pad_token is None:
        tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token

    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        model_id,
        device_map="auto",
        dtype=torch.bfloat16
    )

    # 1. Construct the prompt following the model format
    system_prompt = "You are a professional translator."

    user_prompt = (
        f"Translate the following text from {source_lang} into {target_lang}.\n"
        f"{source_lang}: {text}\n"
        f"{target_lang}:"
    )

    full_prompt = (
        f"<|im_start|>system\n{system_prompt}<|im_end|>\n"
        f"<|im_start|>user\n{user_prompt}<|im_end|>\n"
        f"<|im_start|>assistant\n"
    )

    # 2. Tokenization
    inputs = tokenizer(
        full_prompt,
        return_tensors="pt",
        add_special_tokens=False
    ).to(model.device)

    input_length = inputs.input_ids.shape[1]

    # 3. Generation
    outputs = model.generate(
        inputs.input_ids,
        attention_mask=inputs.attention_mask,
        max_new_tokens=400,
        num_beams=5,
        early_stopping=True,
        pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
        eos_token_id=tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("<|im_end|>")
    )

    # 4. Decoding
    result = tokenizer.decode(
        outputs[0][input_length:],
        skip_special_tokens=True
    )

    return result.replace("<|im_end|>", "").strip()


if __name__ == "__main__":

    # If you want to load the model directly from Hugging Face:
    # model_id = "BSC-LT/salamandraTA-2b-instruct"

    # If the model has already been downloaded locally:
    model_id = "../../models/salamandraTA-2b-instruct"

    src = "English"
    tgt = "Spanish"

    sentence = (
        "Artificial intelligence (AI) is the capability of computational "
        "systems to perform tasks typically associated with human intelligence, "
        "such as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and "
        "decision-making."
    )

    translation = translate_salamandra_manual(
        sentence,
        model_id,
        src,
        tgt
    )

    print(f"\nTranslation: {translation}")

The output should be similar to:

Translation: La inteligencia artificial (IA) es la capacidad de los sistemas computacionales para realizar tareas típicamente asociadas con la inteligencia humana,
tales como el aprendizaje, el razonamiento, la resolución de problemas, la percepción y la toma de decisiones.

There are several important elements in this script.

First, the model is loaded using:

AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained()

Unlike the dedicated NMT models used earlier in the course, SalamandraTA is therefore loaded as a causal language model.

Second, translation is specified through a prompt:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish.
English: [source text]
Spanish:

The script constructs the complete interaction using special delimiters:

<|im_start|>system
You are a professional translator.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
...
<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant

These delimiters identify the different parts of the interaction.

Finally, after generation, the script decodes only the tokens generated after the input prompt:

outputs[0][input_length:]

This prevents the original prompt from being included in the returned translation.

docs.title: 5.1.2. Installing SalamandraTA with MTUOC-server-manager
docs.text:
Once we have verified that the model works independently, we can deploy it through MTUOC-server.

The easiest method is to use MTUOC-server-manager and download the following recipe:

recipe-SalamandraTA.yaml

The recipe downloads the 2B model together with the configuration files required for an English-to-Spanish translation server.

The resulting structure includes the server configuration:

config-server-SalamandraTA.yaml

and, inside the model directory:

salamandraTA-2b-instruct/
└── config-model-SalamandraTA.yaml

The default configuration is prepared for English → Spanish, but both the translation direction and other settings can be adapted.

docs.title: 5.1.3. Server Configuration
docs.text:
Open:

config-server-SalamandraTA.yaml

The file contains:

MTengine: HuggingFace
#download, Marian, Eole, OpusMT, NLLB, HuggingFace, Ollama, GoogleT, DeepL
system_name: SalamandraTA
model_config: ./salamandraTA-2b-instruct/config-model-SalamandraTA.yaml

MTUOCServer:
  port: 8000
  type: MTUOC
  #one of MTUOC, Moses, ModernMT, OpenNMT, NMTWizard
  verbosity_level: 1
  log_file: log.log
  timeout: 45

dopreprocess: False
preprocess_config: None
dotokenization: False
tokenization_config: None
dopostprocess: False
postprocess_config: None

TranslationMemory:
  use: False
  memo: None
  minsim: 100

The most important setting for this exercise is:

MTengine: HuggingFace

This tells MTUOC-server that the model will be loaded using the Hugging Face engine.

The corresponding model configuration is specified here:

model_config: ./salamandraTA-2b-instruct/config-model-SalamandraTA.yaml

Notice that the model configuration is located inside the SalamandraTA model directory.

docs.title: 5.1.4. Model and Prompt Configuration
docs.text:
Now open:

salamandraTA-2b-instruct/config-model-SalamandraTA.yaml

The default configuration is:

prompt_settings:
  template: "Translate the following text from English into Spanish.\nEnglish: {SLsegment}\nSpanish:"
  json_key: None
  regex_pattern: None

model_settings:
  name: "./salamandraTA-2b-instruct"
  device: "cpu"
  #cpu or cuda
  trust_remote_code: true

generation_params:
  max_new_tokens: 512
  temperature: 0.0
  repetition_penalty: 1.2
  top_k: 40
  top_p: 0.9
  no_repeat_ngram_size: 3
  num_beams: 1
  use_eos_token: true
  stop_sequences: ["<|im_end|>", "\nEnglish:", "###"]

The file contains three main groups of parameters:

  1. prompt settings;
  2. model settings;
  3. generation parameters.

docs.title: Prompt Settings
docs.text:
The translation prompt is defined here:

template: "Translate the following text from English into Spanish.\nEnglish: {SLsegment}\nSpanish:"

{SLsegment} is automatically replaced with the source segment received by MTUOC-server.

For example, if the server receives:

This is a translation test.

the prompt becomes:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish.
English: This is a translation test.
Spanish:

The translation direction can therefore be changed by adapting the prompt.

For example, for Spanish-to-English translation:

template: "Translate the following text from Spanish into English.\nSpanish: {SLsegment}\nEnglish:"

The other two prompt settings are:

json_key: None
regex_pattern: None

They can be used when the model returns structured or additional content that needs to be processed. They are not required for the present configuration.

docs.title: Model Settings
docs.text:
The model itself is specified here:

name: "./salamandraTA-2b-instruct"

The device used for inference is configured with:

device: "cpu"

If a compatible GPU is available and the environment has been configured appropriately, this can be changed to:

device: "cuda"

Running the model on a GPU can substantially accelerate inference.

docs.title: Generation Parameters
docs.text:
The final section controls text generation:

generation_params:
  max_new_tokens: 512
  temperature: 0.0
  repetition_penalty: 1.2
  top_k: 40
  top_p: 0.9
  no_repeat_ngram_size: 3
  num_beams: 1
  use_eos_token: true
  stop_sequences: ["<|im_end|>", "\nEnglish:", "###"]

As discussed in Section 4, these parameters influence the model's generation behaviour.

For example:

temperature: 0.0

reduces randomness, while:

max_new_tokens: 512

limits the maximum length of the generated response.

The stop_sequences setting specifies sequences that indicate that generation should stop:

stop_sequences: ["<|im_end|>", "\nEnglish:", "###"]

For this practical exercise, the default values can be retained.

docs.title: 5.1.5. Starting and Testing SalamandraTA
docs.text:
Once the model and configuration files are ready, start MTUOC-server using:

config-server-SalamandraTA.yaml

During startup, MTUOC-server will load the SalamandraTA model specified in the configuration.

Once the server is running, send it an English test segment such as:

Artificial intelligence is changing the translation industry.

The server should return a Spanish translation.

At this point, the complete workflow is:

source segment
      ↓
MTUOC-server
      ↓
translation prompt
      ↓
SalamandraTA
      ↓
generated translation
      ↓
MTUOC-server
      ↓
client application

From the perspective of a CAT tool or another client application, SalamandraTA now behaves as a translation engine accessible through MTUOC-server.

docs.title: 5.1.6. Adapting the Configuration
docs.text:
The recipe provides a working English-to-Spanish configuration, but it can be adapted to different requirements.

The most relevant elements to modify are:

Translation direction

Change the language names in the prompt:

template: "Translate the following text from Spanish into English.\nSpanish: {SLsegment}\nEnglish:"

Device

Use:

device: "cpu"

or, where appropriate:

device: "cuda"

Prompt

Additional instructions can be incorporated using the prompting techniques introduced in Section 4.

For example:

template: "Translate the following text from English into Spanish. Use formal Spanish and provide only the translation.\nEnglish: {SLsegment}\nSpanish:"

This illustrates an important characteristic of LLM-based deployment: the prompt itself becomes part of the translation engine configuration.

docs.title: 5.1.7. Practical Activity
docs.text:
Deploy SalamandraTA through MTUOC-server and perform the following steps:

  1. Download recipe-SalamandraTA.yaml using MTUOC-server-manager.
  2. Locate config-server-SalamandraTA.yaml and config-model-SalamandraTA.yaml.
  3. Check that the model is configured to use the appropriate device (cpu or cuda).
  4. Start MTUOC-server.
  5. Translate several English sentences into Spanish.
  6. Modify the prompt to add one additional translation instruction.
  7. Restart the server if necessary and translate the same sentences again.
  8. Compare the translations produced with the two prompts.

After completing the activity, you should be able to identify the three main elements involved in this deployment:

MTUOC-server configuration
        +
SalamandraTA model
        +
translation prompt

Together, these components turn the locally deployed LLM into a translation service that can be accessed by external applications.

docs.title: 5.2. Gemma
docs.text:
We will now use Gemma, a family of open-weight models developed by Google.

Gemma models are based on research and technology related to Google's Gemini models, but their weights can be downloaded and the models can be run locally. This makes them particularly interesting for experimenting with local LLM deployment and integration into translation workflows.

The Gemma family includes models of different sizes and variants designed for different tasks. In this practical exercise, we will use:

gemma4:e4b

Rather than treating the model as a conventional MT engine, we will explicitly instruct it to translate through a translation prompt. This provides a practical example of the prompting principles introduced in Section 4.

docs.title: 5.2.1. Testing Gemma with Python and Ollama
docs.text:
Before integrating the model into MTUOC-server, we will test it independently. In this example, Gemma will be accessed through Ollama.

Make sure that Ollama is installed and running on your computer. You will also need the Ollama Python library:

pip install ollama

The following Python script sends a translation prompt to the model:

import ollama

# --- OLLAMA SERVER & MODEL SETTINGS ---
MODEL = "gemma4:e4b"
HOST = "http://localhost:11434"

# --- LLM GENERATION PARAMETERS (Ollama Options) ---
generation_params = {
    "temperature": 0.0,
    "num_predict": 128,
    "num_ctx": 2048,
    "repeat_penalty": 1.2,
    "top_k": 40,
    "top_p": 0.9,
    "seed": 42,
    "stop": ["\n", "###"]
}

def executePrompt(prompt):
    try:
        client = ollama.Client(host=HOST)

        response = client.generate(
            model=MODEL,
            prompt=prompt,
            options=generation_params
        )

        output_text = response["response"]

        print("--- Gemma 4 answer ---")
        print(output_text)

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error in connection or generation: {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":

    source_text = "This is an example of translation using a large language model."

    prompt = f"""Translate the following text from English into Spanish.
Provide only the translation.
English: {source_text}"""

    executePrompt(prompt)

If the model and Ollama are working correctly, the output should be similar to:

--- Gemma 4 answer ---
Este es un ejemplo de traducción utilizando un modelo de lenguaje grande.

Notice that the source sentence is incorporated into a prompt:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish.
Provide only the translation.
English: This is an example of translation using a large language model.

The instruction:

Provide only the translation.

is particularly important for integration into an automated workflow. MTUOC-server needs to return the translated segment rather than explanations or additional text generated by the LLM.

The script also defines a set of generation parameters. These control aspects of the model's output, such as maximum generation length, context size, repetition, and token selection.

For translation, the configuration uses:

temperature: 0.0

This reduces randomness in generation and makes the output more deterministic, which is generally desirable when using an LLM as part of a translation workflow.

docs.title: 5.2.2. Installing Gemma with MTUOC-server-manager
docs.text:
Once we have verified that the model works independently, we can integrate it into MTUOC-server.

Use MTUOC-server-manager and download the following recipe:

recipe-ollama-Gemma4.yaml

The recipe creates the configuration files required to connect MTUOC-server to the model running through Ollama.

Two configuration files are particularly important:

config-server-ollama-Gemma4.yaml
config-model-ollama-Gemma4.yaml

They perform different functions:

config-server-ollama-Gemma4.yaml configures MTUOC-server itself and specifies which model configuration should be used.

config-model-ollama-Gemma4.yaml defines how MTUOC-server communicates with Ollama and how the LLM should generate the translation.

docs.title: 5.2.3. Server Configuration
docs.text:
Open:

config-server-ollama-Gemma4.yaml

The configuration is:

MTengine: Ollama
#download, Marian, Eole, OpusMT, NLLB, HuggingFace, Ollama, GoogleT, DeepL
system_name: Ollama
model_config: config-model-ollama-Gemma4.yaml

TranslationMemory:
#path to memory or None
  Path: None
  sl: es
  tl: en

MTUOCServer:
  port: 8000
  type: MTUOC
  #one of MTUOC, Moses, ModernMT, OpenNMT, NMTWizard
  verbosity_level: 1
  log_file: log.log
  timeout: 45

dopreprocess: False
preprocess_config: None
dotokenization: False
tokenization_config: None
dopostprocess: False
postprocess_config: None

The most important line for this exercise is:

MTengine: Ollama

This tells MTUOC-server that translation requests will be handled through Ollama.

The following line identifies the separate model configuration:

model_config: config-model-ollama-Gemma4.yaml

The server configuration determines how MTUOC-server operates, while the model configuration determines which LLM is used and how prompts are sent to it.

docs.title: 5.2.4. Model and Prompt Configuration
docs.text:
Now open:

config-model-ollama-Gemma4.yaml

The complete configuration is:

# --- OLLAMA SERVER & MODEL SETTINGS ---
ollama_settings:
  model: "gemma4:e4b"
  host: "http://localhost:11434"
  timeout: 5

# --- LLM GENERATION PARAMETERS (Ollama Options) ---
generation_params:
  temperature: 0.0
  num_predict: 128
  num_ctx: 2048
  repeat_penalty: 1.2
  top_k: 40
  top_p: 0.9
  seed: 42
  stop: ["\n", "###"]

# --- LLM PROMPT AND RESPONSE PARSING ---
prompt_settings:
  prompt_template: |
    Translate the following text from English into Spanish. Provide only the translation.
    English: {SLsegment}

  json_key: "None"
  regex_pattern: None

The file contains three main groups of settings:

  1. Ollama and model settings;
  2. generation parameters;
  3. prompt and response processing.

docs.title: Ollama Settings
docs.text:
The model is specified here:

model: "gemma4:e4b"

and the location of the Ollama service here:

host: "http://localhost:11434"

In this example, Ollama is running locally on the same computer as MTUOC-server.

docs.title: Generation Parameters
docs.text:
The second part contains the generation parameters used by the model.

For example:

temperature: 0.0

makes generation more deterministic, while:

num_predict: 128

limits the maximum number of tokens generated.

At this stage, you do not need to modify these parameters. The important point is to understand that LLM generation behaviour forms part of the translation engine configuration.

docs.title: Prompt Settings
docs.text:
The translation prompt is defined as:

prompt_template: |
  Translate the following text from English into Spanish. Provide only the translation.
  English: {SLsegment}

{SLsegment} is replaced automatically with the source segment received by MTUOC-server.

For example, if the server receives:

This is an example.

the prompt sent to Gemma becomes:

Translate the following text from English into Spanish. Provide only the translation.
English: This is an example.

This illustrates one of the main differences between the NMT systems used earlier in the course and LLM-based translation:

NMT:
source segment → model

LLM:
source segment → prompt construction → model

The configuration also contains:

json_key: "None"
regex_pattern: None

These options can be used when the model's response needs additional processing.

In this case, no JSON key or regular expression is required because the prompt asks Gemma to return only the translation.

docs.title: 5.2.5. Where Is the Model?
docs.text:
There is an important difference between this configuration and the SalamandraTA configuration.

When using Ollama, there is no model folder inside the MTUOC-server directory.

The model is managed by Ollama and stored in an Ollama-specific directory. The exact location may depend on the operating system and installation method.

MTUOC-server therefore does not load the Gemma model directly from its own directory. Instead, it sends the prompt to the local Ollama service, which manages the model and returns the generated response.

The architecture can be represented as:

CAT tool
   ↓
MTUOC-server
   ↓
Ollama
   ↓
Gemma
   ↓
Ollama
   ↓
MTUOC-server
   ↓
CAT tool

This distinction is useful when troubleshooting the system: MTUOC-server, Ollama, and the LLM are separate components, even though together they behave as a single translation service from the perspective of the CAT tool.

docs.title: 5.2.6. Testing Gemma through MTUOC-server
docs.text:
Once the configuration files are ready and Ollama is running, start MTUOC-server using the Gemma configuration.

Send a test segment to the server and verify that the response contains only the Spanish translation.

For example:

This is an example of translation using a large language model.

should produce a response similar to:

Este es un ejemplo de traducción utilizando un modelo de lenguaje grande.

At this point, the complete workflow is operational:

source segment
      ↓
MTUOC-server
      ↓
translation prompt
      ↓
Ollama
      ↓
Gemma
      ↓
generated translation
      ↓
MTUOC-server
      ↓
client application

You have therefore converted a locally running LLM into a translation service that can be accessed through the same MTUOC-server interface used elsewhere in this course.

docs.title: 5.2.7. Practical Activity
docs.text:
Using the Gemma configuration created in this subsection:

  1. Start Ollama and make sure that gemma4:e4b is available.
  2. Start MTUOC-server with the Gemma configuration.
  3. Translate several English sentences into Spanish.
  4. Check whether Gemma returns only the translation.
  5. Modify the translation prompt by adding one instruction introduced in Section 4, for example:
  6. a terminology requirement;
  7. information about the domain;
  8. a register requirement.
  9. Restart the server if necessary and translate the same sentences again.
  10. Compare the two outputs.

The objective is not simply to obtain a translation, but to observe how the prompt becomes part of the configuration of an LLM-based translation system.

docs.title: 5.3. Comparing the Two Approaches
docs.text:
SalamandraTA and Gemma illustrate two different ways of integrating an open LLM into MTUOC-server.

With SalamandraTA, MTUOC-server uses the Hugging Face engine to load and run the locally stored model directly:

MTUOC-server → Hugging Face engine → SalamandraTA

With Gemma, model execution is managed by Ollama. MTUOC-server communicates with the local Ollama service, which in turn runs the model:

MTUOC-server → Ollama → Gemma

The two configurations can be compared as follows:

SalamandraTA Gemma Model salamandraTA-2b-instruct gemma4:e4b Model type Translation-specific LLM General-purpose LLM MTUOC engine Hugging Face Ollama Model execution Loaded locally through Hugging Face Transformers Managed by Ollama Model location Local model directory Ollama model storage Translation task Translation-oriented model + prompt Defined through the prompt Prompt configuration MTUOC model configuration MTUOC model configuration Generation parameters Configured in YAML Configured in YAML Local execution Yes Yes

Despite these differences, MTUOC-server provides the same external interface to client applications. A CAT tool does not need to know whether the underlying translation is being generated by a model loaded directly through the Hugging Face engine or by a model managed through Ollama.

This illustrates one of the main purposes of MTUOC-server: different translation technologies can be exposed through a common interface and incorporated into the same translation workflow.

It also shows why LLM deployment involves more than simply selecting a model. The complete translation system includes the model, execution framework, prompt, generation parameters, response processing, and server configuration.

Key Takeaways

After completing this section, you should remember that:

  • Open LLMs can be integrated into MTUOC-server and made available to external applications through the same translation interface used for other MT systems.

  • SalamandraTA and Gemma illustrate two different deployment approaches: direct local model loading through the Hugging Face engine and model management through Ollama.

  • In LLM-based translation, the prompt and generation parameters become part of the translation system configuration and determine how source segments are processed and responses are generated.

  • The underlying model and deployment framework remain separate from the client application, allowing different LLM-based translation systems to be integrated into the same MTUOC-server workflow.

docs.title: 6.1. Module Summary
docs.text:
In this module, you have constructed a complete machine translation workflow based on the MTUOC ecosystem.

You first explored the role of MTUOC-server as an interface between translation technologies and client applications. Rather than interacting directly with each translation engine, applications can communicate with MTUOC-server through a common interface.

You then deployed and tested two open neural machine translation approaches:

  • OpusMT, which provides a large collection of models for individual language pairs and multilingual groups;
  • NLLB, a multilingual neural machine translation system designed to support a large number of languages.

In both cases, you first tested the translation model independently and then configured it for use with MTUOC-server.

You subsequently connected MTUOC-server to professional CAT tools, including OmegaT and RWS Trados Studio. This demonstrated how a locally deployed translation system can become part of a professional translation workflow.

The module then introduced the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for translation. Unlike conventional NMT systems, general-purpose LLMs normally require an explicit instruction or prompt specifying the translation task. Prompts can also provide additional information such as context, terminology, examples, register requirements, and output constraints.

Finally, you deployed two LLM-based translation systems:

  • SalamandraTA, a translation-specific model loaded locally through the Hugging Face engine;
  • Gemma, a general-purpose model managed through Ollama.

Despite the differences between these technologies, the overall architecture remains consistent:

translation model
       ↓
MTUOC-server
       ↓
CAT tool
       ↓
translator

The underlying translation technology can therefore change while MTUOC-server continues to provide a common interface to the client application.

docs.title: 6.2. Self-Assessment
docs.text:
Use the following questions to check your understanding of the main concepts and workflows introduced in this module.

Select one answer for each question before opening Show answer.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
1. What is the main function of MTUOC-server?

A. To train neural machine translation models B. To provide an interface between translation technologies and client applications C. To replace CAT tools D. To create translation memories

Show answer

Correct answer: B.

MTUOC-server provides a common interface between translation technologies, such as NMT systems and LLMs, and client applications such as CAT tools.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
2. Which sequence best represents the translation workflow used throughout this module?

A. CAT tool → translator → model → MTUOC-server B. MTUOC-server → model → translator → CAT tool C. Model → MTUOC-server → CAT tool → translator D. Translator → MTUOC-server → model → CAT tool

Show answer

Correct answer: C.

The translation model produces the machine translation, MTUOC-server exposes it through a common interface, the CAT tool integrates the result into the translation environment, and the translator works with the resulting suggestion.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
3. Why is it useful to test an OpusMT or NLLB model independently before integrating it into MTUOC-server?

A. To verify that the model itself works before adding the server layer B. To create a translation memory automatically C. To configure the CAT tool D. To convert the NMT model into an LLM

Show answer

Correct answer: A.

Testing the model independently helps verify that the model and translation direction work correctly before introducing the additional MTUOC-server configuration layer.

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
4. What is an important difference between OpusMT and NLLB?

A. OpusMT can only be used online, while NLLB can only be used locally B. NLLB is an LLM, while OpusMT is an NMT system C. OpusMT provides many models for language pairs or multilingual groups, while NLLB uses a multilingual model covering many languages D. Only OpusMT can be integrated into MTUOC-server

Show answer

Correct answer: C.

OpusMT provides a large collection of models covering individual language pairs and multilingual groups, whereas NLLB uses multilingual models designed to support many languages.

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
5. What makes MTUOC-server useful for integrating machine translation into CAT tools?

A. It converts CAT tools into translation models B. It provides an interface that CAT tools can use to communicate with translation engines C. It removes the need to configure a translation engine D. It automatically post-edits all machine translations

Show answer

Correct answer: B.

MTUOC-server provides an interface through which CAT tools can send source segments to a translation engine and receive translations.

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
6. After a translation model has been successfully connected to MTUOC-server, what is required to use it from a CAT tool?

A. Retrain the translation model from the CAT tool B. Configure the CAT tool to communicate with the running MTUOC-server C. Convert the model into a translation memory D. Install the model directly inside the CAT tool

Show answer

Correct answer: B.

The CAT tool must be configured to communicate with the running MTUOC-server, normally using the appropriate server address and port.

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
7. What is one important difference between conventional NMT and translation with a general-purpose LLM?

A. NMT systems cannot translate complete sentences B. LLMs cannot run locally C. With a general-purpose LLM, the translation task is normally specified through an instruction or prompt D. LLMs do not generate text

Show answer

Correct answer: C.

A general-purpose LLM can perform many different tasks, so translation is normally specified explicitly through an instruction or prompt.

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
8. Which types of information can be incorporated into an LLM translation prompt?

A. Terminology requirements B. Context and register requirements C. Translation examples D. All of the above

Show answer

Correct answer: D.

LLM prompts can include terminology, contextual information, examples, register requirements, output constraints, and other instructions that may influence the translation.

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
9. What is the main deployment difference between SalamandraTA and Gemma in this module?

A. SalamandraTA runs only online, while Gemma runs locally B. SalamandraTA is loaded locally through the Hugging Face engine, while Gemma is managed through Ollama C. SalamandraTA is installed inside the CAT tool, while Gemma is installed inside MTUOC-server D. Gemma does not require MTUOC-server

Show answer

Correct answer: B.

SalamandraTA is loaded locally through the Hugging Face engine, whereas Gemma is managed by Ollama and accessed by MTUOC-server through the local Ollama service.

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
10. What does {SLsegment} represent in an MTUOC-server LLM prompt template?

A. The target language selected by the translator B. The complete translation returned by the model C. The source segment received by MTUOC-server D. The name of the translation model

Show answer

Correct answer: C.

{SLsegment} is replaced automatically with the source segment received by MTUOC-server before the prompt is sent to the LLM.

Key Takeaways

After completing this module, you should remember that:

  • MTUOC-server provides a common interface between translation technologies and client applications.

  • Open NMT models can be selected, tested, configured, and deployed before being integrated into professional CAT-tool workflows.

  • In LLM-based translation, prompts and generation parameters become additional components of the translation system, allowing context, terminology, examples, and other constraints to be incorporated into the translation process.

  • Different translation technologies and deployment frameworks can operate behind the same MTUOC-server interface while the overall professional translation workflow remains consistent.
